## Oral Corticosteroids Reduce Pain After Total Knee Arthroplasty: A Higher Dose of Dexamethasone Effectively Controlled Pain During Motion

A Dose-Response Randomized Placebo-Controlled Trial

Supakit Kanitnate, MD, Yot Tanariyakul, MD, Pattaranatcha Charnwichai, PhD, Pimjai Anthanont, MD, Sudsayam Manuwong, MD, and Nattapol Tammachote, MD, MSc

Investigation performed at Thammasat University Hospital, Pathum Thani, Thailand

Background: Intravenous corticosteroids have been used to manage pain following total knee arthroplasty (TKA). Oral dexamethasone has good bioavailability and is suitable for ambulatory TKA. This study investigated the ef /uniFB01 cacy and dose-response relationship of oral dexamethasone in pain control after TKA.

Methods: In this randomized controlled trial, 120 Thai patients (mean, 68 ± 8 years; 86% female) undergoing primary TKA were allocated to of groups: 16 mg of oral dexamethasone (DEX-16), 8 mg of oral dexamethasone (DEX-8), or placebo. Dexamethasone or placebo was administered once daily, in the morning before surgery and the morning of the /uniFB01 rst postoperative days. The primary outcome was pain at rest and during motion, measured over time. Linear mixed-effects modeling was used to compare outcomes between groups.

Results: Both DEX-8 and DEX-16 signi /uniFB01 cantly reduced pain at rest within hours postoperatively compared with placebo (p < 0.05). However, only DEX-16 signi /uniFB01 cantly reduced pain during motion (p < 0.05). At hours postoperatively, the DEX-16 group showed approximately 50% reductions in pain at rest (p < 0.001) and during motion (p = 0.006) relative to placebo.

Conclusions: Oral dexamethasone was effective in reducing pain after TKA, with a 16-mg dose providing superior pain relief during motion, compared with an 8-mg dose, within the /uniFB01 rst hours. These /uniFB01 ndings support the use of oral dexamethasone as part of multimodal pain management, particularly in an ambulatory TKA setting.

Several studies have shown that corticosteroids are safe when used in appropriately selected patients . The use of corticosteroids for postoperative pain control in joint arthroplasty has gained popularity, with various routes of administration reported .

Dexamethasone is a corticosteroid with potent antiin /uniFB02 ammatory properties . The bioavailability of dexamethasone administered orally is estimated to be approximately 80% relative to the IV route , and oral tablets may be better suited for ambulatory settings.

Participants were allocated in a 1:1:1 ratio. The study was approved by the institutional review board (MTU-EC-OT-6-097/ 62) and registered at ClinicalTrials.gov (NCT04244695). The trial was conducted between January 2020 and March 2023 at Thammasat University Hospital. All participants provided written informed consent.

Inclusion criteria were (1) primary unilateral TKA for osteoarthritis, (2) an age of to years, (3) American Society of Anesthesiologists (ASA) Physical Status I to III, and (4) ability to provide informed consent. ## Intervention and Drug Protocol

Participants took medication pack at 6:00 A.M. on the day of surgery and then each morning for more days. Adherence was monitored by blinded evaluators (S.K., Y.T.). Both participants and evaluators were blinded to the group allocation.

All patients received preemptive analgesia consisting of 0.5 mg of lorazepam and mg of pregabalin the night before and the morning of surgery. Spinal anesthesia was performed using a 27-gauge needle with to mg of 0.5% bupivacaine. Prophylactic cefazolin (2 g) and tranexamic acid (750 mg) were administrated intravenously minutes before surgery. All procedures were performed under the supervision of the same senior surgeon (N.T.), with fellows and residents assisting in every case.

TKA was performed using a medial parapatellar approach with cemented cruciate-retaining implants and patellar resurfacing. A periarticular injection containing mg of 0.5% bupivacaine, 30 mg of ketorolac, 5 mg of morphine sulfate, and 0.6 mg of epinephrine was administered after implantation. An additional 1.5 g of tranexamic acid was injected intra-articularly after wound closure.

Postoperative analgesia included mg of IV ketorolac every hours and mg of IV morphine every hours as needed during the /uniFB01 rst hours. Patients were instructed to request IV morphine administration if visual analog scale (VAS) pain was >30 of points. Patients also received oral naproxen (125 mg) and omeprazole (20 mg) twice daily, acetaminophen (1300 mg) every hours, tramadol (50 mg) every hours, and pregabalin (75 mg) and nortriptyline (25 mg) at bedtime. Patients were discharged on postoperative day (POD) if they met the following criteria: ability to walk at least m with a walker, pain that was well controlled with oral medications, no wound complications, and no urinary retention. Oral medications were continued for weeks postoperatively. Apixaban (2.5 mg) was administered twice daily on PODs through for venous thromboembolism prophylaxis. Follow-up visits occurred at and weeks and months postoperatively.

## Assessments

Patients, surgeons, and evaluators were blinded to the treatment allocation. Postoperative symptoms were recorded by patients or caregivers using standardized forms, collected at discharge and follow-up.

## Statistical Analysis

The required sample size was calculated on the basis of a minimal clinically important difference (MCID) of 20% and a standard deviation estimated from a pilot study of patients. Using an alpha level of 0.05 and power of 0.9, 32 patients per group were required. To account for a 20% dropout rate, 40 participants per group were recruited.

Statistical analyses were conducted using STATA 16.0 (StataCorp). Linear mixed-effects modeling was used to analyze VAS pain scores, opioid consumption, laboratory markers, and functional outcomes. T his study demonstrated that oral dexamethasone effectively reduced pain after TKA. Both the and 16-mg doses improved pain at rest during the /uniFB01 rst hours compared with placebo, while only the 16-mg dose signi /uniFB01 cantly reduced pain during motion. Additionally, the oral dexamethasone lowered in /uniFB02 ammatory markers and caused only a modest rise in blood glucose. A systematic review also found consistent bene /uniFB01 ts regardless of the administration route . As ambulatory TKA becomes increasingly popular, oral options gain importance ; however, oral corticosteroids have been investigated in only a few such studies . Cheng et al. 19 administered mg of oral prednisone daily for days after TKA and reported pain relief through day 28. Shaw et al. 18 compared mg/day of oral dexamethasone (4 mg twice daily) with placebo over days and found a reduction in pain scores that met the MCID only on POD 2. However, their patients also received mg of IV dexamethasone preoperatively, which may have disguised the effect of the oral medication. In contrast, our study excluded IV dexamethasone and showed that multiple oral doses reduced pain within to hours postoperatively, a time frame that is in alignment with a previous report that peak pain occurred within the /uniFB01 rst days following TKA and subsided thereafter .

To our knowledge, this is the /uniFB01 rst study comparing oral dexamethasone doses in this context. Our /uniFB01 ndings indicate that mg was more effective than mg in reducing pain during motion in the early postoperative period. This dosedependent effect is supported by IV studies. Opioid consumption was signi /uniFB01 cantly lower only in the DEX-8 group compared with the placebo group, whereas the difference in the DEX-16 group did not reach signi /uniFB01 cance. These results are inconsistent with previous studies that reported lower opioid use with higher IV dexamethasone doses . In our study, opioid use was generally low across all groups, likely due to the use of a multimodal analgesia protocol. Prior metaanalyses also found that perioperative dexamethasone reduced morphine use and the PONV rate after TKA .

Corticosteroids are known to exert strong antiin /uniFB02 ammatory effects. In our study, both DEX groups had lower CRP levels on PODs and than the placebo group, with a stronger effect observed in the higher-dose group. This supports prior /uniFB01 ndings that IV dexamethasone suppressed in /uniFB02 ammatory markers after TKA . By weeks, however, CRP levels normalized across groups.

Hyperglycemia is a well-recognized concern following systemic glucocorticoid use. Glucose levels of >180 mg/dL may impair leukocyte function and increase the risk of infection . However, large cohort studies and meta-analyses have not found an association of dexamethasone use with increased infection risk . Kheir et al. 30 identi /uniFB01 ed mg/dL as the FBS threshold for elevated PJI risk. In our study, the DEX-16 group exhibited approximately 12% higher FBS, but levels stayed below the threshold. Consistent with earlier reports , transient hyperglycemia occurred without an increased PJI rate.

Hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis suppression by dexamethasone is another consideration. A study in healthy volunteers reported transient HPA suppression within hours following a single 8-mg dose of IV dexamethasone . However, another study found no signi /uniFB01 cant suppression with perioperative doses of to mg . Prednisolone at doses of >5 mg/day for <2 weeks is generally low risk with respect to adrenal suppression . Even in patients with lymphoma receiving mg/day of prednisolone for days, adrenal suppression resolved within days . Our regimen of mg of oral dexamethasone daily (equivalent to approximately mg of prednisolone) for days also falls within this low-risk range.

Participants were allocated in a 1:1:1 ratio. The study was approved by the institutional review board (MTU-EC-OT-6-097/ 62) and registered at ClinicalTrials.gov (NCT04244695). The trial was conducted between January 2020 and March 2023 at Thammasat University Hospital. All participants provided written informed consent.

Inclusion criteria were (1) primary unilateral TKA for osteoarthritis, (2) an age of to years, (3) American Society of Anesthesiologists (ASA) Physical Status I to III, and (4) ability to provide informed consent. Exclusion criteria included (1) uncontrolled diabetes (hemoglobin A1c of >7.0%), (2) a body mass index (BMI) of >40 kg/m , (3) in /uniFB02 ammatory joint disease, (4) systemic corticosteroid use within months previously, (5) a history of peptic ulcer hemorrhage, (6) cognitive or psychiatric impairment affecting pain assessment, (7) severe renal dysfunction (glomerular /uniFB01 ltration rate [GFR] of <30 mL/min/1.73 m 2 ) or hepatic dysfunction (Child-Pugh class C), (8) prior opioid abuse, and (9) allergy to any of the study medications.

The DEX-16 group received mg of oral dexamethasone daily for days (a total of mg), the DEX-8 group received mg of oral dexamethasone daily for days (a total of mg), and the placebo group received placebo tablets. ## Intervention and Drug Protocol

Participants took medication pack at 6:00 A.M. on the day of surgery and then each morning for more days. Adherence was monitored by blinded evaluators (S.K., Y.T.). Both participants and evaluators were blinded to the group allocation.

All patients received preemptive analgesia consisting of 0.5 mg of lorazepam and mg of pregabalin the night before and the morning of surgery. Spinal anesthesia was performed using a 27-gauge needle with to mg of 0.5% bupivacaine. Prophylactic cefazolin (2 g) and tranexamic acid (750 mg) were administrated intravenously minutes before surgery. All procedures were performed under the supervision of the same senior surgeon (N.T.), with fellows and residents assisting in every case.

TKA was performed using a medial parapatellar approach with cemented cruciate-retaining implants and patellar resurfacing. A periarticular injection containing mg of 0.5% bupivacaine, 30 mg of ketorolac, 5 mg of morphine sulfate, and 0.6 mg of epinephrine was administered after implantation. An additional 1.5 g of tranexamic acid was injected intra-articularly after wound closure.

Postoperative analgesia included mg of IV ketorolac every hours and mg of IV morphine every hours as needed during the /uniFB01 rst hours. Patients were instructed to request IV morphine administration if visual analog scale (VAS) pain was >30 of points. Patients also received oral naproxen (125 mg) and omeprazole (20 mg) twice daily, acetaminophen (1300 mg) every hours, tramadol (50 mg) every hours, and pregabalin (75 mg) and nortriptyline (25 mg) at bedtime. Patients were discharged on postoperative day (POD) if they met the following criteria: ability to walk at least m with a walker, pain that was well controlled with oral medications, no wound complications, and no urinary retention. Oral medications were continued for weeks postoperatively. Apixaban (2.5 mg) was administered twice daily on PODs through for venous thromboembolism prophylaxis. Follow-up visits occurred at and weeks and months postoperatively.

Patients, surgeons, and evaluators were blinded to the treatment allocation. Postoperative symptoms were recorded by patients or caregivers using standardized forms, collected at discharge and follow-up.

## Statistical Analysis

The required sample size was calculated on the basis of a minimal clinically important difference (MCID) of 20% and a standard deviation estimated from a pilot study of patients. Using an alpha level of 0.05 and power of 0.9, 32 patients per group were required. To account for a 20% dropout rate, 40 participants per group were recruited.

Statistical analyses were conducted using STATA 16.0 (StataCorp). Linear mixed-effects modeling was used to analyze VAS pain scores, opioid consumption, laboratory markers, and functional outcomes. When a global F-test indicated a signi /uniFB01 cant difference among the groups, post hoc comparisons were performed using least signi /uniFB01 cant difference (LSD) tests. ## Discussion

T his study demonstrated that oral dexamethasone effectively reduced pain after TKA. Both the and 16-mg doses improved pain at rest during the /uniFB01 rst hours compared with placebo, while only the 16-mg dose signi /uniFB01 cantly reduced pain during motion. Additionally, the oral dexamethasone lowered in /uniFB02 ammatory markers and caused only a modest rise in blood glucose. Early functional outcomes were comparable across all groups within the /uniFB01 rst months postoperatively.

Dexamethasone has been incorporated into multimodal analgesia protocols after TKA, and many studies have con/uniFB01 rmed the analgesic ef /uniFB01 cacy of IV dexamethasone by comparison with placebo after TKA . A systematic review also found consistent bene /uniFB01 ts regardless of the administration route . As ambulatory TKA becomes increasingly popular, oral options gain importance ; however, oral corticosteroids have been investigated in only a few such studies . Cheng et al. 19 administered mg of oral prednisone daily for days after TKA and reported pain relief through day 28. Shaw et al. 18 compared mg/day of oral dexamethasone (4 mg twice daily) with placebo over days and found a reduction in pain scores that met the MCID only on POD 2. However, their patients also received mg of IV dexamethasone preoperatively, which may have disguised the effect of the oral medication. In contrast, our study excluded IV dexamethasone and showed that multiple oral doses reduced pain within to hours postoperatively, a time frame that is in alignment with a previous report that peak pain occurred within the /uniFB01 rst days following TKA and subsided thereafter .

To our knowledge, this is the /uniFB01 rst study comparing oral dexamethasone doses in this context. Our /uniFB01 ndings indicate that mg was more effective than mg in reducing pain during motion in the early postoperative period. This dosedependent effect is supported by IV studies. Hyperglycemia is a well-recognized concern following systemic glucocorticoid use. Glucose levels of >180 mg/dL may impair leukocyte function and increase the risk of infection . Background: Tranexamic acid (TXA) and absorbable hemostat (AH) are widely used to reduce perioperative blood loss in total knee arthroplasty (TKA). This study tested the ef /uniFB01 cacy and safety of TXA combined with AH for perioperative blood management in TKA.

Methods: Hemostatic ef /uniFB01 cacy was preliminarily evaluated through in vitro dynamic coagulation assays, lactate dehydrogenase activity measurements, and scanning electron microscopy, as well as in vivo using a rabbit liver bleeding model. The in vivo biocompatibility was also measured. Subsequently, the ef /uniFB01 cacy and safety of TXA combined with AH were further evaluated in a prospective, blinded study involving individuals who were randomized to receive TXA, AH, or TXA AH during TKA. The primary outcomes were perioperative blood loss, blood transfusion, hemoglobin and hematocrit levels, maximum hemoglobin change, anemia, and postoperative complications. Secondary outcomes included perioperative in /uniFB02 ammation, coagulation function, and knee joint function.

Results: Coagulation assays and the liver hemostasis model demonstrated that TXA combined with AH effectively promoted coagulation, with satisfactory biocompatibility. The clinical results of Han Chinese (East Asian) patients indicated that the combination signi /uniFB01 cantly reduced perioperative blood loss in TKA (564.51 ± 136.26 mL in the TXA AH group, 879.35 ± 85.62 mL in the TXA group, and 692.70 ± 96.06 mL in the AH group; p < 0.001) without an increase in thromboembolic events or wound-related complications. Conclusions: The combination of TXA and AH effectively reduced perioperative blood loss in TKA, accelerated early patient recovery, and did not increase the rate of complications.

K nee osteoarthritis is a chronic degenerative disease that severely impacts patient quality of life as the disease progresses to advanced stages . At present, total knee arthroplasty (TKA) is considered the gold-standard treatment for end-stage osteoarthritic conditions . However, it often necessitates extensive soft-tissue dissection and cancellous bone osteotomy, resulting in substantial perioperative blood loss of up to to mL, which is approximately 10% to 20% of total circulating blood volume . Excessive blood loss not only slows postoperative recovery but also adversely affects surgical outcomes . This is particularly problematic for elderly patients with poor physiological compensation and reserve capacity, as it often leads to severe complications. Additionally, the need for transfusion due to blood loss introduces risks and exacerbates the shortage of blood resources . Therefore, implementing effective hemostatic measures is crucial to enhancing recovery after TKA .

At present, tranexamic acid (TXA) is the most commonly used hemostatic agent in the TKA perioperative period. TXA that is locally injected prior to the closure of the joint cavity inhibits /uniFB01 brinolysis and effectively reduces perioperative blood loss by competitively binding to lysine sites on plasminogen . Moreover, studies have also shown that the application of TXA does not increase the incidence of thromboembolic complications . However, the ef /uniFB01 cacy of TXA application remains suboptimal due to rapid TXA loss and the quick absorption of residual TXA by local vascular cells, resulting in failure to maintain effective drug concentrations, as well as compromised hemostatic ef /uniFB01 cacy . Given that enhanced recovery after surgery protocols demand greater perioperative hemostasis, relying solely on TXA is inadequate, and further optimization and enhancement are necessary.

Absorbable hemostat (AH) is another widely used hemostatic strategy in clinical practice. Unlike the anti /uniFB01 brinolytic mechanism of TXA, AH exerts local hemostatic effects through physical and chemical pathways . Upon contact with blood, AH causes erythrocyte destruction, exposing hemoglobin. The carboxyl groups in AH further oxidize hemoglobin to hematin, releasing ferric ions that accelerate platelet aggregation and adhesion, leading to the formation of a hemostatic thrombus . Additionally, by providing a scaffold for platelet adhesion and aggregation and enabling the formation of a gelatinous mass through its water-absorbing property, AH effectively controls bleeding from capillaries, venules, and arterioles -which can prove challenging when using conventional hemostatic measures . Given the different hemostatic stages and mechanisms of TXA and AH, their combined use may offer complementary effects. AH can also serve as a scaffold to adsorb TXA, preventing rapid local loss. Unfortunately, there is a lack of solid evidence regarding the combined application of TXA and AH in TKA.

Therefore, we explored the hemostatic effect and safety of TXA combined with AH through in vitro dynamic coagulation tests and a rabbit liver local-bleeding model. Subsequently, we conducted a randomized controlled trial to evaluate the clinical ef /uniFB01 cacy and safety of TXA combined with AH in reducing perioperative blood loss in TKA. Through this study, we hope to provide new strategies for accelerating patient recovery.

## In Vitro Coagulation Test

The procoagulant properties of plain gauze (PG) (Henan Kelong Medical Apparatus & Instruments), PG TXA (China Resources Double-Crane Pharmaceutical), oxidized cellulosebased AH (SURGICEL; Johnson & Johnson), and TXA AH were /uniFB01 rst evaluated by measuring the blood clotting index (BCI). Subsequently, the cellular adhesion of various hemostatic materials was evaluated using scanning electron microscopy (SEM) and lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) enzyme activity assays. Detailed methods are provided in the Appendix.

## In Vivo Liver Hemostasis Assay and Biocompatibility Assessment

New Zealand rabbits were immobilized in the supine position following anesthesia. After exposing the liver, a 1-cm-long and 5-mm-deep incision was made on its surface. Hemostatic materials were immediately applied over the incision. Bleeding time and blood loss were meticulously recorded. Two days postoperatively, blood samples were collected for routine blood and biochemical analysis to evaluate the in vivo biocompatibility. See the Appendix for detailed methods.

## Patient Recruitment

Patients admitted to our hospital from March to September 2023 were included if they were to years of age; had an American Society of Anesthesiologists (ASA) functional status of I, II, or III; underwent TKA for primary end-stage knee osteoarthritis; and consented to participate in the trial. Exclusion criteria included diagnoses other than primary osteoarthritis, preoperative anemia, an allergy to AH or TXA, anticoagulant use within days before surgery, a history of hematological disorders or venous thrombosis, or a body mass index (BMI) of >35 kg/m . All patients provided informed consent for participation.

## Outcomes and Follow-up

Demographic data and outcomes were collected from electronic medical records. The primary outcomes included total perioperative, intraoperative, and hidden blood loss; hemoglobin and hematocrit levels; maximum hemoglobin change; the rate of anemia; the number and volume of transfusions; venous thromboembolism; wound-related complications; and other serious adverse events . The secondary outcomes included platelet count, activated partial thromboplastin time (APTT), prothrombin time (PT), erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR), C-reactive protein (CRP) level, interleukin-6 (IL-6) level, Ddimer level, /uniFB01 brinogen level, knee circumference, knee mobility, HSS knee score, VAS pain score, stride speed, liver and kidney function, and other adverse events. All patients were followed for >6 months postoperatively. The measurement methods are detailed in the Supplementary Materials and illustrated in Figure S1 (see Appendix).

## Statistical Analysis

Continuous data are presented as the mean ± standard deviation and were compared using an analysis of variance, with Tukey honestly signi /uniFB01 cant difference (HSD) tests for pairwise comparisons. Categorical data are presented as counts and percentages, and differences among groups were assessed using chisquare or Kruskal-Wallis tests, with the Bonferroni correction for multiple comparisons. A power analysis of the outcomes was also performed (see Appendix Table S1). With a signi /uniFB01 cance level of 0.05 and a power of 0.8, 36 patients were required in each group. Anticipating a loss to follow-up rate of 10%, 40 patients were included in the study. All analyses were conducted using R software (version 4.4.2; R Foundation for Statistical Computing).

## Patient Selection and Baseline Characteristics

Of the patients enrolled, 20 did not meet the inclusion criteria and did not provide consent. The remaining patients were randomized into the TXA, AH, and TXA AH groups. Two patients in the AH group and in the TXA AH group refused follow-up due to transportation issues, while and patients in each group, respectively, were lost to followup for unclear reasons, resulting in Han Chinese (East Asian) patients eligible for the analysis (Fig. 4). All patients were followed for >6 months. There were no signi /uniFB01 cant differences in baseline characteristics among the groups (Table I).

## Clinical Outcomes

Among the primary outcomes, total perioperative and hidden blood loss were signi /uniFB01 cantly lower in the TXA AH group compared with the TXA and AH groups, whereas intraoperative blood loss was similar between the TXA AH and AH groups but was notably lower in those groups compared with the TXA group (Figs. 5-A, 5-B, and 5-C). Accordingly, hemoglobin and hematocrit levels on postoperative days and were signi /uniFB01 -cantly higher in the TXA AH group compared with the other groups (Figs. 5-D and 5-E). There were no signi /uniFB01 cant differences in postoperative transfusion rates or volumes. However, patients in the TXA AH group had a signi /uniFB01 cantly lower incidence of postoperative anemia than the other groups, and the proportion of patients with moderate to severe anemia was also signi /uniFB01 cantly lower in the TXA AH group. No differences in venous thromboembolism, wound-related complications, or other serious adverse events were observed among the groups (Table II).

With respect to the secondary outcomes, platelet counts were signi /uniFB01 cantly higher in the TXA AH group than in the TXA group on both postoperative days and and were signi /uniFB01 cantly higher in the AH group than in the TXA group on postoperative day (Fig. 6-A). Nevertheless, the other coagulation-related parameters, including APTT, PT, D-dimer, and /uniFB01 brinogen, remained consistent among all groups. No differences were observed in liver and kidney function or other adverse events among the groups (see Appendix Fig. S2). In terms of functional recovery, the TXA AH group demonstrated a signi /uniFB01 cantly higher range of motion than the TXA group (Fig. 6-B). More importantly, the TXA AH group exhibited a signi /uniFB01 cantly higher HSS score than both the TXA and AH groups on postoperative day and maintained a signi /uniFB01 cant advantage over the TXA group on postoperative day (Fig. 6-C). Similarly, stride speed in the TXA AH group was signi /uniFB01 cantly higher than that in both the TXA and AH groups on postoperative day and remained signi /uniFB01 cantly superior to that in the TXA group on postoperative day (Fig. 6-D). Finally, the combination of TXA and AH more effectively alleviated knee swelling after surgery compared with TXA alone, while no signi /uniFB01 cant difference in VAS pain was observed among the groups (Table III).

## Discussion

D uring TKA, the implementation of effective and safe hemostatic strategies is crucial to enhancing recovery after surgery . Since a single hemostatic measure is insuf /uniFB01 -cient to meet clinical needs, this study explored the combined use of TXA and AH. Through laboratory experiments and a randomized controlled trial, the ef /uniFB01 cacy and safety of this combination were synergistically validated. The results indicate that the combination of TXA and AH further reduced perioperative blood loss in TKA compared with TXA or AH alone, without increasing

Regarding safety, we found that the combination did not increase the risks of deep venous thrombosis and pulmonary embolism, which are the most serious complications of TXA use. Additionally, since AH serves as a scaffolding material to bind TXA through physical adsorption and intermolecular forces such as ionic and hydrogen bonds, the combination could avoid the rapid loss of TXA during surgery, thereby preventing the need for high-dose TXA, as well as the related side effects. Nevertheless, combining TXA with AH may alter the pharmacokinetic characteristics of TXA itself. Herein, we veri /uniFB01 ed that such a combination caused no additional adverse effects on key organs (the liver and kidney) involved in drug metabolism. Previous studies have linked AH-related complications to factors such as AH size, local blood /uniFB02 ow, placement location, and whether the AH is removed after hemostasis .

In a review of the application of AH in surgery, Franceschini reported that surgical site infections, allergic reactions, foreign body reactions, and nerve compression are common postoperative issues . In the present study, no signi /uniFB01 cant abnormalities were observed in in /uniFB02 ammatory markers or wound healing in the AH and TXA AH groups, indicating that local, rational use of AH, with strict adherence to usage indications, is safe when combined with TXA.

This study has limitations. First, it only included patients with primary knee osteoarthritis and did not evaluate other types of patients undergoing TKA. ## Ef /uniFB01 cacy and Safety of Tranexamic Acid Combined with Absorbable Hemostat in Reducing Perioperative Blood Loss in Total Knee Arthroplasty

A Prospective, Blinded, Randomized Controlled Trial

Qing-Yi Zhang, MD*, Gang Wang, MM*, Jun-Hong Qu, MD, Ye Li, MD, Hong-Jun Peng, MM, Steve T.L. Pambayi, MM, Jing Yang, MD, Yi Zeng, MD, and Bin Shen, MD

Investigation performed at the Department of Orthopedics and Orthopedic Research Institute, West China Hospital, Sichuan University, Chengdu 610041, People ' s Republic of China

Background: Tranexamic acid (TXA) and absorbable hemostat (AH) are widely used to reduce perioperative blood loss in total knee arthroplasty (TKA). However, the ef /uniFB01 cacy of single-method hemostatic strategies is increasingly insuf /uniFB01 cient for meeting clinical demands. This study tested the ef /uniFB01 cacy and safety of TXA combined with AH for perioperative blood management in TKA.

Methods: Hemostatic ef /uniFB01 cacy was preliminarily evaluated through in vitro dynamic coagulation assays, lactate dehydrogenase activity measurements, and scanning electron microscopy, as well as in vivo using a rabbit liver bleeding model. The in vivo biocompatibility was also measured. Subsequently, the ef /uniFB01 cacy and safety of TXA combined with AH were further evaluated in a prospective, blinded study involving individuals who were randomized to receive TXA, AH, or TXA AH during TKA. The primary outcomes were perioperative blood loss, blood transfusion, hemoglobin and hematocrit levels, maximum hemoglobin change, anemia, and postoperative complications. Secondary outcomes included perioperative in /uniFB02 ammation, coagulation function, and knee joint function.

Results: Coagulation assays and the liver hemostasis model demonstrated that TXA combined with AH effectively promoted coagulation, with satisfactory biocompatibility. The clinical results of Han Chinese (East Asian) patients indicated that the combination signi /uniFB01 cantly reduced perioperative blood loss in TKA (564.51 ± 136.26 mL in the TXA AH group, 879.35 ± 85.62 mL in the TXA group, and 692.70 ± 96.06 mL in the AH group; p < 0.001) without an increase in thromboembolic events or wound-related complications. Additionally, the combination accelerated early postoperative knee function recovery without signi /uniFB01 cantly affecting pain scores or in /uniFB02 ammatory markers.

Conclusions: The combination of TXA and AH effectively reduced perioperative blood loss in TKA, accelerated early patient recovery, and did not increase the rate of complications.

K nee osteoarthritis is a chronic degenerative disease that severely impacts patient quality of life as the disease progresses to advanced stages . At present, total knee arthroplasty (TKA) is considered the gold-standard treatment for end-stage osteoarthritic conditions . However, it often necessitates extensive soft-tissue dissection and cancellous bone osteotomy, resulting in substantial perioperative blood loss of up to to mL, which is approximately 10% to 20% of total circulating blood volume . Excessive blood loss not only slows postoperative recovery but also adversely affects surgical outcomes . This is particularly problematic for elderly patients with poor physiological compensation and reserve capacity, as it often leads to severe complications. Additionally, the need for transfusion due to blood loss introduces risks and exacerbates the shortage of blood resources . Therefore, implementing effective hemostatic measures is crucial to enhancing recovery after TKA .

At present, tranexamic acid (TXA) is the most commonly used hemostatic agent in the TKA perioperative period. TXA that is locally injected prior to the closure of the joint cavity inhibits /uniFB01 brinolysis and effectively reduces perioperative blood loss by competitively binding to lysine sites on plasminogen . Moreover, studies have also shown that the application of TXA does not increase the incidence of thromboembolic complications . However, the ef /uniFB01 cacy of TXA application remains suboptimal due to rapid TXA loss and the quick absorption of residual TXA by local vascular cells, resulting in failure to maintain effective drug concentrations, as well as compromised hemostatic ef /uniFB01 cacy . Given that enhanced recovery after surgery protocols demand greater perioperative hemostasis, relying solely on TXA is inadequate, and further optimization and enhancement are necessary.

Absorbable hemostat (AH) is another widely used hemostatic strategy in clinical practice. Unlike the anti /uniFB01 brinolytic mechanism of TXA, AH exerts local hemostatic effects through physical and chemical pathways . Upon contact with blood, AH causes erythrocyte destruction, exposing hemoglobin. The carboxyl groups in AH further oxidize hemoglobin to hematin, releasing ferric ions that accelerate platelet aggregation and adhesion, leading to the formation of a hemostatic thrombus . Additionally, by providing a scaffold for platelet adhesion and aggregation and enabling the formation of a gelatinous mass through its water-absorbing property, AH effectively controls bleeding from capillaries, venules, and arterioles -which can prove challenging when using conventional hemostatic measures . Given the different hemostatic stages and mechanisms of TXA and AH, their combined use may offer complementary effects. AH can also serve as a scaffold to adsorb TXA, preventing rapid local loss. Unfortunately, there is a lack of solid evidence regarding the combined application of TXA and AH in TKA.

Therefore, we explored the hemostatic effect and safety of TXA combined with AH through in vitro dynamic coagulation tests and a rabbit liver local-bleeding model. Subsequently, we conducted a randomized controlled trial to evaluate the clinical ef /uniFB01 cacy and safety of TXA combined with AH in reducing perioperative blood loss in TKA. Through this study, we hope to provide new strategies for accelerating patient recovery.

## Materials and Methods

T he study protocols were approved by the ethics committee of our institution and registered in the Chinese Clinical Trial Registry (ChiCTR2300071664). We later updated the registry information and implemented partial modi /uniFB01 cations to the outcome classi /uniFB01 cations. The primary outcomes consisted of direct measures of the ef /uniFB01 cacy and safety of TXA and AH combination therapy -speci /uniFB01 cally, perioperative blood loss volume, transfusion requirements, the rate of anemia, hemoglobin and hematocrit levels, and the occurrences of wound complications, thromboembolic events, and other serious adverse events. Indirect measures were classi /uniFB01 ed as secondary outcomes and included functional recovery parameters (joint range of motion, stride speed, Hospital for Special Surgery [HSS] knee score, and visual analogue scale [VAS] pain score), systemic in /uniFB02 ammatory and coagulation biomarkers, and other data related to complications. The relevant updated information can be accessed on the registry platform. Additionally, this study was conducted and reported in strict adherence to the Consolidated Standards Of Reporting Trials (CONSORT) statement (see Appendix).

## In Vitro Coagulation Test

The procoagulant properties of plain gauze (PG) (Henan Kelong Medical Apparatus & Instruments), PG TXA (China Resources Double-Crane Pharmaceutical), oxidized cellulosebased AH (SURGICEL; Johnson & Johnson), and TXA AH were /uniFB01 rst evaluated by measuring the blood clotting index (BCI). Subsequently, the cellular adhesion of various hemostatic materials was evaluated using scanning electron microscopy (SEM) and lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) enzyme activity assays. Detailed methods are provided in the Appendix.

## In Vivo Liver Hemostasis Assay and Biocompatibility Assessment

New Zealand rabbits were immobilized in the supine position following anesthesia. After exposing the liver, a 1-cm-long and 5-mm-deep incision was made on its surface. Hemostatic materials were immediately applied over the incision. Bleeding time and blood loss were meticulously recorded. Two days postoperatively, blood samples were collected for routine blood and biochemical analysis to evaluate the in vivo biocompatibility. See the Appendix for detailed methods.

## Patient Recruitment

Patients admitted to our hospital from March to September 2023 were included if they were to years of age; had an American Society of Anesthesiologists (ASA) functional status of I, II, or III; underwent TKA for primary end-stage knee osteoarthritis; and consented to participate in the trial. Exclusion criteria included diagnoses other than primary osteoarthritis, preoperative anemia, an allergy to AH or TXA, anticoagulant use within days before surgery, a history of hematological disorders or venous thrombosis, or a body mass index (BMI) of >35 kg/m . All patients provided informed consent for participation.

## Outcomes and Follow-up

Demographic data and outcomes were collected from electronic medical records. The primary outcomes included total perioperative, intraoperative, and hidden blood loss; hemoglobin and hematocrit levels; maximum hemoglobin change; the rate of anemia; the number and volume of transfusions; venous thromboembolism; wound-related complications; and other serious adverse events . The secondary outcomes included platelet count, activated partial thromboplastin time (APTT), prothrombin time (PT), erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR), C-reactive protein (CRP) level, interleukin-6 (IL-6) level, Ddimer level, /uniFB01 brinogen level, knee circumference, knee mobility, HSS knee score, VAS pain score, stride speed, liver and kidney function, and other adverse events. All patients were followed for >6 months postoperatively. The measurement methods are detailed in the Supplementary Materials and illustrated in Figure S1 (see Appendix).

## Statistical Analysis

Continuous data are presented as the mean ± standard deviation and were compared using an analysis of variance, with Tukey honestly signi /uniFB01 cant difference (HSD) tests for pairwise comparisons. Categorical data are presented as counts and percentages, and differences among groups were assessed using chisquare or Kruskal-Wallis tests, with the Bonferroni correction for multiple comparisons. A power analysis of the outcomes was also performed (see Appendix Table S1). With a signi /uniFB01 cance level of 0.05 and a power of 0.8, 36 patients were required in each group. Anticipating a loss to follow-up rate of 10%, 40 patients were included in the study. All analyses were conducted using R software (version 4.4.2; R Foundation for Statistical Computing).

## Patient Selection and Baseline Characteristics

Of the patients enrolled, 20 did not meet the inclusion criteria and did not provide consent. The remaining patients were randomized into the TXA, AH, and TXA AH groups. Two patients in the AH group and in the TXA AH group refused follow-up due to transportation issues, while and patients in each group, respectively, were lost to followup for unclear reasons, resulting in Han Chinese (East Asian) patients eligible for the analysis (Fig. 4). All patients were followed for >6 months. There were no signi /uniFB01 cant differences in baseline characteristics among the groups (Table I).

## Clinical Outcomes

Among the primary outcomes, total perioperative and hidden blood loss were signi /uniFB01 cantly lower in the TXA AH group compared with the TXA and AH groups, whereas intraoperative blood loss was similar between the TXA AH and AH groups but was notably lower in those groups compared with the TXA group (Figs. 5-A, 5-B, and 5-C). Accordingly, hemoglobin and hematocrit levels on postoperative days and were signi /uniFB01 -cantly higher in the TXA AH group compared with the other groups (Figs. 5-D and 5-E). There were no signi /uniFB01 cant differences in postoperative transfusion rates or volumes. However, patients in the TXA AH group had a signi /uniFB01 cantly lower incidence of postoperative anemia than the other groups, and the proportion of patients with moderate to severe anemia was also signi /uniFB01 cantly lower in the TXA AH group. No differences in venous thromboembolism, wound-related complications, or other serious adverse events were observed among the groups (Table II).

With respect to the secondary outcomes, platelet counts were signi /uniFB01 cantly higher in the TXA AH group than in the TXA group on both postoperative days and and were signi /uniFB01 cantly higher in the AH group than in the TXA group on postoperative day (Fig. 6-A). Nevertheless, the other coagulation-related parameters, including APTT, PT, D-dimer, and /uniFB01 brinogen, remained consistent among all groups. No differences were observed in liver and kidney function or other adverse events among the groups (see Appendix Fig. S2). In terms of functional recovery, the TXA AH group demonstrated a signi /uniFB01 cantly higher range of motion than the TXA group (Fig. 6-B). More importantly, the TXA AH group exhibited a signi /uniFB01 cantly higher HSS score than both the TXA and AH groups on postoperative day and maintained a signi /uniFB01 cant advantage over the TXA group on postoperative day (Fig. 6-C). Similarly, stride speed in the TXA AH group was signi /uniFB01 cantly higher than that in both the TXA and AH groups on postoperative day and remained signi /uniFB01 cantly superior to that in the TXA group on postoperative day (Fig. 6-D). Finally, the combination of TXA and AH more effectively alleviated knee swelling after surgery compared with TXA alone, while no signi /uniFB01 cant difference in VAS pain was observed among the groups (Table III).

## Discussion

D uring TKA, the implementation of effective and safe hemostatic strategies is crucial to enhancing recovery after surgery . Since a single hemostatic measure is insuf /uniFB01 -cient to meet clinical needs, this study explored the combined use of TXA and AH. Through laboratory experiments and a randomized controlled trial, the ef /uniFB01 cacy and safety of this combination were synergistically validated. Regarding safety, we found that the combination did not increase the risks of deep venous thrombosis and pulmonary embolism, which are the most serious complications of TXA use. Additionally, since AH serves as a scaffolding material to bind TXA through physical adsorption and intermolecular forces such as ionic and hydrogen bonds, the combination could avoid the rapid loss of TXA during surgery, thereby preventing the need for high-dose TXA, as well as the related side effects. Nevertheless, combining TXA with AH may alter the pharmacokinetic characteristics of TXA itself. Herein, we veri /uniFB01 ed that such a combination caused no additional adverse effects on key organs (the liver and kidney) involved in drug metabolism. Previous studies have linked AH-related complications to factors such as AH size, local blood /uniFB02 ow, placement location, and whether the AH is removed after hemostasis .

In a review of the application of AH in surgery, Franceschini reported that surgical site infections, allergic reactions, foreign body reactions, and nerve compression are common postoperative issues . In the present study, no signi /uniFB01 cant abnormalities were observed in in /uniFB02 ammatory markers or wound healing in the AH and TXA AH groups, indicating that local, rational use of AH, with strict adherence to usage indications, is safe when combined with TXA.

## Behavioral Intervention to Foster Healthy Lifestyle Physical Activity After Complex Lumbar Surgery

## A Randomized Controlled Trial

Carol A. Mancuso, MD, Roland Duculan, MD, Manuela C. Lafage, BSN, Frank P. Cammisa, MD, Andrew A. Sama, MD, Alexander P. Hughes, MD, Darren R. Lebl, MD, and Federico P. Girardi, MD

Investigation performed at the Hospital for Special Surgery, New York, NY

Background: Persistent sedentary lifestyles are prevalent after complex lumbar surgery. Inactivity often is due to habit, is not necessary, and results in both adverse general health and adverse spine health. We tested a multicomponent behavioral intervention administered in surgical practices to increase lifestyle walking after recuperation from surgery involving ‡ 3 lumbar levels or fusion. This analysis reports the main objective of measuring change in physical activity; subsequent analysis will address the additional objective of measuring change in disability due to lumbar pain.

Methods: At months postoperatively, patients were interviewed in person, completed the self-reported Paffenbarger Physical Activity and Exercise Index measuring energy expenditure in kcal/week from walking and total activity, and were randomized to the control or a behavioral intervention. Patients in the intervention group made a contract to increase walking and received a pedometer and information about activity bene /uniFB01 ts, followed by telephone contacts over year to reinforce the intervention and assess activity change. Controls received only information about activity bene /uniFB01 ts and fewer telephone contacts to assess activity change. The primary outcome was the difference in within-patient change in kcal/week from walking (as measured by the Paffenbarger Index) from enrollment to months later. Additional assessments and outcomes included changes in the total Paffenbarger Index from enrollment to and months and changes in the walking domain to months.

Results: Among patients (mean age, 63 years; 53% men; 96% White patients and 6% Latino patients), 123 received the intervention and were controls. The mean energy expenditure from walking increased from enrollment to months for patients in the intervention group (1,437 to kcal/week; p < 0.0001) and for controls (1,320 to kcal/week; p < 0.0001), with a greater difference for the intervention group (1,165 compared with kcal/week; p = 0.03). At months, the effectiveness of the intervention was sustained (estimated effect, 588 kcal/week [95% con /uniFB01 dence interval (CI), 119 to kcal/week]; p = 0.01) when accounting for new events that potentially affect activity, such as another lumbar surgery (estimate, 2 1,396 kcal/week [95% CI, 2 2,116 to 2 676 kcal/week]; p = 0.0002) and new arthroplasty or foot or ankle surgery (estimate, 2 701 kcal/week [95% CI, 2 1,212 to 2 189 kcal/week]; p = 0.007). Similar results were obtained for changes in total activity. Retention in this study was 92%; 72% of all patients reported that being in the study did not affect spine symptoms, and 28% reported that being in the study made symptoms better. No adverse events were associated with the trial.

Conclusions: A behavioral intervention was effective in increasing lifestyle walking after recuperation from complex lumbar surgery. These /uniFB01 ndings support integrating counseling about physical activity into routine postoperative care in surgical practices.

P hysical activity is essential for both general health and spine health . In addition to fostering muscle strength and bone formation, prudent activity promotes proper alignment and weight maintenance, which are necessary for the postoperative lumbar spine.

Painful lumbar disorders are known to lead to avoiding physical activity and adopting lifestyles that are sedentary (i.e., mostly sitting or lying down) . Interestingly, although acknowledging the bene /uniFB01 ts of activity, many patients remain inactive postoperatively, with activity levels below population norms . Covariates and reasons for persistent inactivity include residual pain, fear of injury, more complex surgery, and depressive symptoms . These factors are superimposed on a background of general reasons for inactivity, including age, comorbidity, body mass index, habit, and life circumstances that encroach on access to or time for activity .

Behavioral interventions are known to effectively increase physical activity in patients with musculoskeletal conditions . These interventions, based on precepts such as the social cognitive theory, involve providing information about the bene /uniFB01 ts of physical activity, increasing self-ef /uniFB01 cacy (i.e., the con /uniFB01 dence or belief in the ability to succeed in a situation), setting activity goals, providing ongoing approbation and positive feedback from study personnel for healthy behaviors, and physiology feedback of success as would be provided by a motion-sensing device such as a pedometer . Outcomes are often self-reported as time spent in activities or energy expenditure in kilocalories per week. It is not known whether such interventions would be effective in patients after complex lumbar surgery.

To address this question, we conducted a trial to foster physical activity, taking into account several issues. First, patients need approbation from surgeons that physical activity is good for the spine; therefore, we conducted the trial in spine practices after surgeons af /uniFB01 rmed that it was safe for each patient to increase physical activity. Second, introducing an intervention postoperatively, rather than preoperatively, would be more logical, as patients would not be limited by the most severe pain or distracted by concerns about surgery. Third, the activity should be something that everyone could do safely, such as increased lifestyle walking integrated into daily routines. Fourth, on the basis of prior studies, we selected a 4month outcome, given that it is not possible to continually increase activity inde /uniFB01 nitely, to assess the effectiveness of implementing the intervention and a 12-month outcome to assess the effectiveness of maintaining the intervention . Fifth, to account for the role of social interaction in fostering behavior change, the comparator group should be an attention control group and receive a prespeci /uniFB01 ed protocol of interactions with study personnel.

## Materials and Methods

T his trial was approved by our institutional review board, and all patients provided written informed consent. Consecutive patients of participating surgeons were screened, enrolled, and interviewed in person during routine 3-month postoperative visits. Patients were eligible if they had had complex lumbar surgery based on the validated Surgical Invasiveness Index, which considers the number of vertebral levels involved, decompression, fusion with or without instrumentation, and approach ; were ‡ 18 years of age; and spoke English; and if their surgeon con /uniFB01 rmed that it was safe to increase lifestyle walking. Patients were excluded if they reported cardiopulmonary symptoms on a physical activity preparticipation screening questionnaire . The study was registered at ClinicalTrials.gov (NCT02611427). This analysis reports the main objective of measuring change in physical activity; subsequent analysis will address the additional objective of measuring change in disability due to lumbar pain.

## Information from Patients at Enrollment

Patients self-reported their age, sex, race, and ethnicity. Patients completed the Paffenbarger Physical Activity and Exercise Index, an epidemiological measure of physical activity in domains . Patients were asked how many blocks they walked daily, how many stairs they climbed daily, and the frequency and duration of sports and exercise during the past week. If walking was reported in miles, a conversion of mile = 20 blocks was made. Weekly energy expenditure in kcal/week was calculated on the basis of a standard compendium that assigns kilocalories to different activities and sports and considers the amount of the activity and sport performed . For example, walking blocks daily corresponds to kcal/week (i.e., 20 blocks/day · 8 kcal/block · 7 days/week). Coupling the Paffenbarger Index and the compendium provided a comprehensive self-reported account of baseline and within-patient change in energy expenditure. The kcal/week were calculated for each domain and were summed to represent total physical activity. Patients also reported their previous activity behaviors (i.e., participation in sports or exercise years ago and when they were teenagers or young adults).

Using validated surveys, patients were asked about medical conditions (Charlson Comorbidity Index), depressive symptoms (Patient Health Questionnaire-8 [PHQ-8]), pain-related disability (Oswestry Disability Index), and fear of increasing back pain (Fear-Avoidance Beliefs Questionnaire) . After completing all surveys, patients were randomized 1:1 to either the control or intervention group according to a blocked sequence, unknown to the recruiting investigators, of initially and then patients. Randomization was not strati /uniFB01 ed for any variable, and assignments were provided to recruiting investigators at the time of each enrollment.

## Intervention Group

Patients in the intervention group received a multicomponent behavioral intervention based on social cognitive theory . First, patients were given the 2008 Physical Activity Guidelines for Americans, and sections on increasing lifestyle walking were emphasized . Second, to increase self-ef /uniFB01 cacy or self-con /uniFB01 dence, patients described prior challenging life events that they successfully overcame. Third, patients made a contract to increase walking that they were con /uniFB01 dent they could ful /uniFB01 ll (e.g., how many more blocks/day, incorporating more walking into daily routines). Patients could also report walking in terms of miles (including on a treadmill), and this was then converted as above. Patients in the intervention group were also given a DIGI WALKER pedometer (Yamax), which has been validated by the manufacturer during treadmill testing and free-living walking . For patients in our trial, the pedometer was calibrated to individual stride length and was used to provide physiological evidence of successfully walking more.

Patients in the intervention group were contacted by telephone weekly, and then biweekly, for months and then monthly up to months to receive approbation or positive feedback from study personnel and to report interval outcome data (each contact was approximately minutes). ## Attention Control Group

Patients in the control group received the 2008 Physical Activity Guidelines for Americans, and study personnel emphasized increasing lifestyle walking . Patients were contacted by telephone monthly up to months. Three major time points were similarly de /uniFB01 ned around 4, 8, and 12-month assessments and outcomes. Patients in the control group could receive a total of contacts within the 4-month period and contacts within the 12-month period.

## Definition of Outcomes

The primary outcome was the difference between groups in the within-patient change, from enrollment to months, in energy expenditure (kcal/week) from blocks walked, as measured by the Paffenbarger Index. A secondary outcome was the difference between groups in the within-patient change in total kcal/ week (sum of all Paffenbarger Index domains) from enrollment to months. Additional secondary outcomes were the differences between groups in the within-patient change in kcal/ week from blocks walked and in total kcal/week at months. A validated self-reported outcome was used instead of a wearable device, which often is not systematically worn for the long term.

## Blinding

Patients were blinded to the randomization group. In order to enhance rapport and foster using pedometers and ful /uniFB01 llment of walking contracts, the same investigators enrolled patients, conducted telephone interviews, and administered follow-up questionnaires.

## Clinical Information

Medical records were reviewed for operative details to classify surgical complexity .

## Information from Patients During Follow-ups

During each telephone contact, patients in both groups were asked about untoward events from increased walking (e.g., back pain, muscle and/or joint symptoms, new or worsening medical conditions). Both groups completed the Paffenbarger Index again at 4, 8, and months. Suggestions were offered for indoor walking if weather hindered outdoor activity. Patients also were asked about any new clinical or personal life events that impeded activity efforts. Responses were grouped into spine-related events (e.g., another lumbar surgery), lower-extremity events

(e.g., hip and knee arthroplasty, foot and ankle surgery), and other musculoskeletal, medical, or personal events. At the /uniFB01 nal follow-up, patients were asked how participation in this trial affected the spine symptoms (i.e., no effect, symptoms were better, or symptoms were worse).

## Sample Size

The sample size was based on the 4-month outcome. In prior longitudinal studies, standard deviations for weekly energy expenditure ranged from to kcal/week and an increase in kcal/week (equivalent to blocks/day) corresponded to decreased cardiovascular risk . Using a standard deviation of kcal/week, a goal of detecting a difference of kcal/week (equivalent to blocks/day), an alpha of 0.05, and a power of 90%, we required patients per group. Assuming attrition of 15%, 122 patients per group (244 total) were required.

## Results

F rom November 2015 to February 2018, 364 consecutive patients were screened; 260 were enrolled, and were randomized to the control and were randomized to the intervention (Fig. 1). Nine patients withdrew (due to unhappiness with the surgical outcome, no time, pressing family matters), and patient died (not related to the trial). Thus, 127 patients in the control group and patients in the intervention group were eligible for follow-ups. Patients who did or did not withdraw were similar in Paffenbarger Index values and demographic and clinical characteristics (p > 0.05 for all comparisons).

The mean age (and standard deviation) of the entire sample was 63 ± 11 years, 132 patients (53%) were men, 241 (96%) were White, 15 (6%) were Latino, and the mean time since surgery was 2.9 ± 0.4 months. Randomization was successful, with similar demographic and clinical characteristics (Table I) and Paffenbarger Index values (Table II) between groups and according to surgeon.

## Primary Outcome at Months

For the patients in the intervention group, 114 completed the Paffenbarger Index at a mean of 4.2 ± 0.5 months; of these patients, 89 (78%) had ‡ 6 of the possible telephone contacts. For the patients in the control group, 111 completed the Paffenbarger Index at a mean of 4.2 ± 0.6 months; of these patients, 95 (86%) had ‡ 3 of the possible telephone contacts.

The mean kcal/week for the walking domain had increased at months for each group (p < 0.0001; paired t test), but the increase was greater for the intervention group (p = 0.03) (Table II). Greater kcal/week for the intervention group were also found for the 4-month difference in total physical activity (Tables II and III).

## Secondary Outcomes

Follow-up Paffenbarger Index values were obtained for the 8month outcome (89 patients in the control group and patients in the intervention group) and the 12-month outcome (122 patients in the control group and patients in the intervention group), resulting in 92% retention. The /uniFB01 nal mean follow-up time was 12.7 ± 1.3 months for the control group and 12.5 ± 1.2 months for the intervention group. Longitudinal results demonstrate that the initial 4-month walking and total activity gains were sustained during the longer-term follow-up period (Fig. 2). However, 95% con /uniFB01 -dence intervals overlapped for all values, indicating that there were wide variations within groups.

Throughout the trial, all patients reported life events that occurred since enrollment that they perceived impeded physical activity, including another lumbar surgery in patients (12%) and lower-extremity surgery (hip and knee arthroplasty or foot or ankle surgery) in patients (30%). In multivariable models, the intervention remained associated with greater kcal/week, and the reported events were associated with fewer kcal/week for the 12-month walking and total activity outcomes (Table III).

The pedometer was used to provide physiological feedback of measurable change. At the 12-month follow-up, 59% of patients in the intervention group reported that the pedometer was helpful at the beginning of the trial, 16% reported that it was helpful throughout the trial, and 25% reported that it was not helpful.

## Adverse Events

At months, 66% of patients in the intervention group and 78% of patients in the control group reported that being in the trial had no effect on the spine symptoms, and 34% of patients in the intervention group and 22% of patients in the control group reported that being in the trial made the spine symptoms better (odds ratio [OR], 1.8 [95% con /uniFB01 dence interval (CI), 1.0 to 3.2]; p = 0.05). There were no trial-related adverse events reported in either group.

## Discussion

A multicomponent behavioral intervention to increase physical activity after initial recuperation from complex lumbar surgery was effective in increasing kcal/week from walking and from total activities after months, and the gain was sustained at months. These gains were achieved without worsening spine symptoms. This trial builds on our prior work identifying patient-reported barriers to physical activity and offers an effective intervention based on established behavioral principles .

Our trial can impact patient care in several ways. First, our results highlight that walking more, compared with formal exercise, is a practical behavior that patients willingly accept. Second, fostering physical activity should not be restricted to primary-care settings but should be integrated into spine surgery practices where maximizing future spine health is a priority. Third, surgeons should be aware that subsequent surgical procedures can derail patients from physical activity; thus, reinforcing physical activity should be part of routine followup care.

We enrolled patients several months postoperatively when they had recuperated suf /uniFB01 ciently and would potentially be motivated to resume active lifestyles (i.e., at a teachable moment when individuals are more receptive to behavior change) . Approval from surgeons provided con /uniFB01 rmation not only that it was safe to increase activity but also that it was advisable. This type of approbation cannot be duplicated by other health-care providers who are not knowledgeable about the nature and/or extent of surgery and may be reluctant to persuade patients to increase activity. Thus, our trial supports including what otherwise would be a general health intervention into surgical practice.

We found wide variations in activity levels throughout the trial for both groups. These variations likely re /uniFB02 ected other variables associated with inactivity that we did not account for, such as availability of places to walk, the family ' s fear of injury, and seasonal variations. Future studies should address these issues as well as account for the history of physical activity, include longer follow-ups, and include new motion-tracking devices and technologies that patients prefer (i.e., other than a pedometer). Future studies also could ascertain which components of the intervention are most effective for this population and clinical scenario.

We found peak activity levels at around months and then modest declines. This /uniFB01 nding is consistent with the wellknown challenges of sustaining activity gains and the possible

need for a booster to reinforce behavior . In future studies, such boosters could be administered with reapplication of the initial intervention. This would be pertinent in our sample because intervening life events, such as other surgeries impacting mobility, were prevalent.

Previous reports considering physical activity after lumbar surgery were mostly observational and did not include behavioral interventions. Some studies assessed self-reported walking dif /uniFB01 culty and performance-based measures, such as gait speed, and reported improvements compared with preoperative status . These studies identi /uniFB01 ed multiple covariates, including age, comorbidity, disability, body mass index, fear-avoidance, and surgical complexity . Among longitudinal studies, peak improvements were reported at to months postoperatively, followed by sustained improvements or moderate decreases at months .

Our study had several limitations that could be addressed in future research. First, this study was conducted at a single urban Northeast tertiary-care center with primarily White patients and may not be applicable to other patients in different settings. Second, to administer the intervention longitudinally and maintain rapport with patients, study personnel were not blinded to the randomization group. This strategy did result in excellent retention rates. Third, we relied on a self-reported scale to measure activity. However, this scale is well-established and has been widely used in epidemiologic studies of physical activity. Fourth, although patients were given the same rehabilitation protocol, we did not quantify the duration or intensity of postoperative physical therapy. Fifth, we did not track other activity-related outcomes such as weight.

In summary, in this randomized controlled trial of patients enrolled months after complex lumbar surgery, a multicomponent behavioral intervention was effective in increasing physical activity, primarily lifestyle walking, 4 months after enrollment and bene /uniFB01 ts were sustained to months. These /uniFB01 ndings support counseling patients during routine postoperative care to increase physical activity in order to enhance both general health and spine health. n

## Behavioral Intervention to Foster Healthy Lifestyle Physical Activity After Complex Lumbar Surgery

## A Randomized Controlled Trial

Carol A. Mancuso, MD, Roland Duculan, MD, Manuela C. Lafage, BSN, Frank P. Cammisa, MD, Andrew A. Sama, MD, Alexander P. Hughes, MD, Darren R. Lebl, MD, and Federico P. Girardi, MD

Investigation performed at the Hospital for Special Surgery, New York, NY

Background: Persistent sedentary lifestyles are prevalent after complex lumbar surgery. Inactivity often is due to habit, is not necessary, and results in both adverse general health and adverse spine health. We tested a multicomponent behavioral intervention administered in surgical practices to increase lifestyle walking after recuperation from surgery involving ‡ 3 lumbar levels or fusion. This analysis reports the main objective of measuring change in physical activity; subsequent analysis will address the additional objective of measuring change in disability due to lumbar pain.

Methods: At months postoperatively, patients were interviewed in person, completed the self-reported Paffenbarger Physical Activity and Exercise Index measuring energy expenditure in kcal/week from walking and total activity, and were randomized to the control or a behavioral intervention. Patients in the intervention group made a contract to increase walking and received a pedometer and information about activity bene /uniFB01 ts, followed by telephone contacts over year to reinforce the intervention and assess activity change. Controls received only information about activity bene /uniFB01 ts and fewer telephone contacts to assess activity change. The primary outcome was the difference in within-patient change in kcal/week from walking (as measured by the Paffenbarger Index) from enrollment to months later. Additional assessments and outcomes included changes in the total Paffenbarger Index from enrollment to and months and changes in the walking domain to months.

Results: Among patients (mean age, 63 years; 53% men; 96% White patients and 6% Latino patients), 123 received the intervention and were controls. The mean energy expenditure from walking increased from enrollment to months for patients in the intervention group (1,437 to kcal/week; p < 0.0001) and for controls (1,320 to kcal/week; p < 0.0001), with a greater difference for the intervention group (1,165 compared with kcal/week; p = 0.03). At months, the effectiveness of the intervention was sustained (estimated effect, 588 kcal/week [95% con /uniFB01 dence interval (CI), 119 to kcal/week]; p = 0.01) when accounting for new events that potentially affect activity, such as another lumbar surgery (estimate, 2 1,396 kcal/week [95% CI, 2 2,116 to 2 676 kcal/week]; p = 0.0002) and new arthroplasty or foot or ankle surgery (estimate, 2 701 kcal/week [95% CI, 2 1,212 to 2 189 kcal/week]; p = 0.007). Similar results were obtained for changes in total activity. Retention in this study was 92%; 72% of all patients reported that being in the study did not affect spine symptoms, and 28% reported that being in the study made symptoms better. No adverse events were associated with the trial.

Conclusions: A behavioral intervention was effective in increasing lifestyle walking after recuperation from complex lumbar surgery. These /uniFB01 ndings support integrating counseling about physical activity into routine postoperative care in surgical practices.

P hysical activity is essential for both general health and spine health . In addition to fostering muscle strength and bone formation, prudent activity promotes proper alignment and weight maintenance, which are necessary for the postoperative lumbar spine.

Painful lumbar disorders are known to lead to avoiding physical activity and adopting lifestyles that are sedentary (i.e., mostly sitting or lying down) . Interestingly, although acknowledging the bene /uniFB01 ts of activity, many patients remain inactive postoperatively, with activity levels below population norms . Covariates and reasons for persistent inactivity include residual pain, fear of injury, more complex surgery, and depressive symptoms . These factors are superimposed on a background of general reasons for inactivity, including age, comorbidity, body mass index, habit, and life circumstances that encroach on access to or time for activity .

Behavioral interventions are known to effectively increase physical activity in patients with musculoskeletal conditions . These interventions, based on precepts such as the social cognitive theory, involve providing information about the bene /uniFB01 ts of physical activity, increasing self-ef /uniFB01 cacy (i.e., the con /uniFB01 dence or belief in the ability to succeed in a situation), setting activity goals, providing ongoing approbation and positive feedback from study personnel for healthy behaviors, and physiology feedback of success as would be provided by a motion-sensing device such as a pedometer . Outcomes are often self-reported as time spent in activities or energy expenditure in kilocalories per week. It is not known whether such interventions would be effective in patients after complex lumbar surgery.

To address this question, we conducted a trial to foster physical activity, taking into account several issues. First, patients need approbation from surgeons that physical activity is good for the spine; therefore, we conducted the trial in spine practices after surgeons af /uniFB01 rmed that it was safe for each patient to increase physical activity. Second, introducing an intervention postoperatively, rather than preoperatively, would be more logical, as patients would not be limited by the most severe pain or distracted by concerns about surgery. Third, the activity should be something that everyone could do safely, such as increased lifestyle walking integrated into daily routines. Fourth, on the basis of prior studies, we selected a 4month outcome, given that it is not possible to continually increase activity inde /uniFB01 nitely, to assess the effectiveness of implementing the intervention and a 12-month outcome to assess the effectiveness of maintaining the intervention . Fifth, to account for the role of social interaction in fostering behavior change, the comparator group should be an attention control group and receive a prespeci /uniFB01 ed protocol of interactions with study personnel.

The study question was whether a behavioral intervention instituted during a randomized trial after complex lumbar surgery would be effective in improving self-reported physical activity. The hypothesis was that a multicomponent psychosocial behavioral intervention would be effective in increas-

## Materials and Methods

T his trial was approved by our institutional review board, and all patients provided written informed consent. Consecutive patients of participating surgeons were screened, enrolled, and interviewed in person during routine 3-month postoperative visits. Patients were eligible if they had had complex lumbar surgery based on the validated Surgical Invasiveness Index, which considers the number of vertebral levels involved, decompression, fusion with or without instrumentation, and approach ; were ‡ 18 years of age; and spoke English; and if their surgeon con /uniFB01 rmed that it was safe to increase lifestyle walking. Patients were excluded if they reported cardiopulmonary symptoms on a physical activity preparticipation screening questionnaire . The study was registered at ClinicalTrials.gov (NCT02611427). This analysis reports the main objective of measuring change in physical activity; subsequent analysis will address the additional objective of measuring change in disability due to lumbar pain.

## Information from Patients at Enrollment

Patients self-reported their age, sex, race, and ethnicity. Patients completed the Paffenbarger Physical Activity and Exercise Index, an epidemiological measure of physical activity in domains . Patients were asked how many blocks they walked daily, how many stairs they climbed daily, and the frequency and duration of sports and exercise during the past week. If walking was reported in miles, a conversion of mile = 20 blocks was made. Weekly energy expenditure in kcal/week was calculated on the basis of a standard compendium that assigns kilocalories to different activities and sports and considers the amount of the activity and sport performed . For example, walking blocks daily corresponds to kcal/week (i.e., 20 blocks/day · 8 kcal/block · 7 days/week). Coupling the Paffenbarger Index and the compendium provided a comprehensive self-reported account of baseline and within-patient change in energy expenditure. The kcal/week were calculated for each domain and were summed to represent total physical activity. Patients also reported their previous activity behaviors (i.e., participation in sports or exercise years ago and when they were teenagers or young adults).

Using validated surveys, patients were asked about medical conditions (Charlson Comorbidity Index), depressive symptoms (Patient Health Questionnaire-8 [PHQ-8]), pain-related disability (Oswestry Disability Index), and fear of increasing back pain (Fear-Avoidance Beliefs Questionnaire) . After completing all surveys, patients were randomized 1:1 to either the control or intervention group according to a blocked sequence, unknown to the recruiting investigators, of initially and then patients. Randomization was not strati /uniFB01 ed for any variable, and assignments were provided to recruiting investigators at the time of each enrollment.

## Intervention Group

Patients in the intervention group received a multicomponent behavioral intervention based on social cognitive theory . First, patients were given the 2008 Physical Activity Guidelines for Americans, and sections on increasing lifestyle walking were emphasized . Second, to increase self-ef /uniFB01 cacy or self-con /uniFB01 dence, patients described prior challenging life events that they successfully overcame. Third, patients made a contract to increase walking that they were con /uniFB01 dent they could ful /uniFB01 ll (e.g., how many more blocks/day, incorporating more walking into daily routines). Patients could also report walking in terms of miles (including on a treadmill), and this was then converted as above. Patients in the intervention group were also given a DIGI WALKER pedometer (Yamax), which has been validated by the manufacturer during treadmill testing and free-living walking . For patients in our trial, the pedometer was calibrated to individual stride length and was used to provide physiological evidence of successfully walking more.

Patients in the intervention group were contacted by telephone weekly, and then biweekly, for months and then monthly up to months to receive approbation or positive feedback from study personnel and to report interval outcome data (each contact was approximately minutes). ## Definition of Outcomes

The primary outcome was the difference between groups in the within-patient change, from enrollment to months, in energy expenditure (kcal/week) from blocks walked, as measured by the Paffenbarger Index. A secondary outcome was the difference between groups in the within-patient change in total kcal/ week (sum of all Paffenbarger Index domains) from enrollment to months. Additional secondary outcomes were the differences between groups in the within-patient change in kcal/ week from blocks walked and in total kcal/week at months. A validated self-reported outcome was used instead of a wearable device, which often is not systematically worn for the long term.
