## Blinding

Patients were blinded to the randomization group. In order to enhance rapport and foster using pedometers and ful /uniFB01 llment of walking contracts, the same investigators enrolled patients, conducted telephone interviews, and administered follow-up questionnaires.

## Clinical Information

Medical records were reviewed for operative details to classify surgical complexity .

## Information from Patients During Follow-ups

During each telephone contact, patients in both groups were asked about untoward events from increased walking (e.g., back pain, muscle and/or joint symptoms, new or worsening medical conditions). Both groups completed the Paffenbarger Index again at 4, 8, and months. Suggestions were offered for indoor walking if weather hindered outdoor activity. Patients also were asked about any new clinical or personal life events that impeded activity efforts. Responses were grouped into spine-related events (e.g., another lumbar surgery), lower-extremity events

(e.g., hip and knee arthroplasty, foot and ankle surgery), and other musculoskeletal, medical, or personal events. At the /uniFB01 nal follow-up, patients were asked how participation in this trial affected the spine symptoms (i.e., no effect, symptoms were better, or symptoms were worse).

## Sample Size

The sample size was based on the 4-month outcome. In prior longitudinal studies, standard deviations for weekly energy expenditure ranged from to kcal/week and an increase in kcal/week (equivalent to blocks/day) corresponded to decreased cardiovascular risk . Using a standard deviation of kcal/week, a goal of detecting a difference of kcal/week (equivalent to blocks/day), an alpha of 0.05, and a power of 90%, we required patients per group. Assuming attrition of 15%, 122 patients per group (244 total) were required.

## Results

F rom November 2015 to February 2018, 364 consecutive patients were screened; 260 were enrolled, and were randomized to the control and were randomized to the intervention (Fig. 1). Nine patients withdrew (due to unhappiness with the surgical outcome, no time, pressing family matters), and patient died (not related to the trial). Thus, 127 patients in the control group and patients in the intervention group were eligible for follow-ups. Patients who did or did not withdraw were similar in Paffenbarger Index values and demographic and clinical characteristics (p > 0.05 for all comparisons).

The mean age (and standard deviation) of the entire sample was 63 ± 11 years, 132 patients (53%) were men, 241 (96%) were White, 15 (6%) were Latino, and the mean time since surgery was 2.9 ± 0.4 months. Randomization was successful, with similar demographic and clinical characteristics (Table I) and Paffenbarger Index values (Table II) between groups and according to surgeon.

## Primary Outcome at Months

For the patients in the intervention group, 114 completed the Paffenbarger Index at a mean of 4.2 ± 0.5 months; of these patients, 89 (78%) had ‡ 6 of the possible telephone contacts. For the patients in the control group, 111 completed the Paffenbarger Index at a mean of 4.2 ± 0.6 months; of these patients, 95 (86%) had ‡ 3 of the possible telephone contacts.

The mean kcal/week for the walking domain had increased at months for each group (p < 0.0001; paired t test), but the increase was greater for the intervention group (p = 0.03) (Table II). Greater kcal/week for the intervention group were also found for the 4-month difference in total physical activity (Tables II and III).

## Secondary Outcomes

Follow-up Paffenbarger Index values were obtained for the 8month outcome (89 patients in the control group and patients in the intervention group) and the 12-month outcome (122 patients in the control group and patients in the intervention group), resulting in 92% retention. The /uniFB01 nal mean follow-up time was 12.7 ± 1.3 months for the control group and 12.5 ± 1.2 months for the intervention group. Longitudinal results demonstrate that the initial 4-month walking and total activity gains were sustained during the longer-term follow-up period (Fig. 2). However, 95% con /uniFB01 -dence intervals overlapped for all values, indicating that there were wide variations within groups.

Throughout the trial, all patients reported life events that occurred since enrollment that they perceived impeded physical activity, including another lumbar surgery in patients (12%) and lower-extremity surgery (hip and knee arthroplasty or foot or ankle surgery) in patients (30%). In multivariable models, the intervention remained associated with greater kcal/week, and the reported events were associated with fewer kcal/week for the 12-month walking and total activity outcomes (Table III).

The pedometer was used to provide physiological feedback of measurable change. At the 12-month follow-up, 59% of patients in the intervention group reported that the pedometer was helpful at the beginning of the trial, 16% reported that it was helpful throughout the trial, and 25% reported that it was not helpful.

## Adverse Events

At months, 66% of patients in the intervention group and 78% of patients in the control group reported that being in the trial had no effect on the spine symptoms, and 34% of patients in the intervention group and 22% of patients in the control group reported that being in the trial made the spine symptoms better (odds ratio [OR], 1.8 [95% con /uniFB01 dence interval (CI), 1.0 to 3.2]; p = 0.05). There were no trial-related adverse events reported in either group.

## Discussion

A multicomponent behavioral intervention to increase physical activity after initial recuperation from complex lumbar surgery was effective in increasing kcal/week from walking and from total activities after months, and the gain was sustained at months. These gains were achieved without worsening spine symptoms. This trial builds on our prior work identifying patient-reported barriers to physical activity and offers an effective intervention based on established behavioral principles .

Our trial can impact patient care in several ways. First, our results highlight that walking more, compared with formal exercise, is a practical behavior that patients willingly accept. Second, fostering physical activity should not be restricted to primary-care settings but should be integrated into spine surgery practices where maximizing future spine health is a priority. Third, surgeons should be aware that subsequent surgical procedures can derail patients from physical activity; thus, reinforcing physical activity should be part of routine followup care.

We enrolled patients several months postoperatively when they had recuperated suf /uniFB01 ciently and would potentially be motivated to resume active lifestyles (i.e., at a teachable moment when individuals are more receptive to behavior change) . Approval from surgeons provided con /uniFB01 rmation not only that it was safe to increase activity but also that it was advisable. This type of approbation cannot be duplicated by other health-care providers who are not knowledgeable about the nature and/or extent of surgery and may be reluctant to persuade patients to increase activity. Thus, our trial supports including what otherwise would be a general health intervention into surgical practice.

We found wide variations in activity levels throughout the trial for both groups. These variations likely re /uniFB02 ected other variables associated with inactivity that we did not account for, such as availability of places to walk, the family ' s fear of injury, and seasonal variations. Future studies should address these issues as well as account for the history of physical activity, include longer follow-ups, and include new motion-tracking devices and technologies that patients prefer (i.e., other than a pedometer). Future studies also could ascertain which components of the intervention are most effective for this population and clinical scenario.

We found peak activity levels at around months and then modest declines. This /uniFB01 nding is consistent with the wellknown challenges of sustaining activity gains and the possible

hc_limitations:
Our study had several limitations that could be addressed in future research. First, this study was conducted at a single urban Northeast tertiary-care center with primarily White patients and may not be applicable to other patients in different settings. Second, to administer the intervention longitudinally and maintain rapport with patients, study personnel were not blinded to the randomization group. This strategy did result in excellent retention rates. Third, we relied on a self-reported scale to measure activity. However, this scale is well-established and has been widely used in epidemiologic studies of physical activity. Fourth, although patients were given the same rehabilitation protocol, we did not quantify the duration or intensity of postoperative physical therapy. Fifth, we did not track other activity-related outcomes such as weight.

This study aimed to evaluate the correlation of preoperative cognitive and psychological factors with POD after TKA. Methods: This prospective cohort study included patients who were ‡ 60 years of age and underwent primary TKA at of major tertiary care hospitals. Psychological assessments were conducted with the Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index (PSQI), the Patient Health Questionnaire-15 (PHQ-15), and the Hospital Anxiety and Depression Scale (HADS). Although cognitive impairment is a well-established risk factor for POD, most studies have relied on brief assessments such as the Mini-Mental State Examination (MMSE), which fail to capture the full spectrum of cognitive functions . Additionally, preoperative psychological symptoms such as sleep disturbances, anxiety, and depression have been linked to an increased risk of POD . Given the high prevalence of these conditions among elderly patients undergoing TKA , a comprehensive assessment of cognitive and psychological functions is crucial for identifying modi /uniFB01 able preoperative risk factors and developing targeted interventions to prevent POD . Recent systematic reviews have further underscored this need, emphasizing the multifactorial nature of POD and noting that most available evidence derives from heterogeneous surgical cohorts rather than TKA populations speci /uniFB01 cally . Consequently, in this study we hypothesized that speci /uniFB01 c aspects of cognitive and psychological functions may increase the risk of POD in patients undergoing TKA. Additionally, it evaluated preoperative cognitive and psychological functions and their correlation with POD, while integrating a comprehensive spectrum of potential risk factors, such as comorbidities, laboratory /uniFB01 ndings, baseline medication usage, and environmental factors. Materials and Methods The attending physicians reviewed each patient ' s medical history, explained the study to them, and obtained their informed consent day prior to surgery. On the same day, research evaluators who had undergone standardized training from the principal investigator conducted cognitive and psychological assessments. These evaluators also collected demographic and clinical information, data on socioeconomic factors, laboratory results, and environmental conditions before surgery. Cognitive function was evaluated using the Korean version of the Consortium to Establish a Registry for Alzheimer ' s Disease (CERAD) neuropsychological battery, which comprises tests: J1 (Verbal Fluency), J2 (Boston Naming Test), J3 (MMSE), J4 (Wordlist Learning), J5 (Constructional Praxis), J6 (Wordlist Recall), J7 (Wordlist Recognition), J8 (Constructional Praxis Recall), and J9 (Trail Making Test, Parts A and B) . The CERAD total II score was calculated by summing the J1, J2, J4, J5, J6, J7, and J8 scores. Subjective cognitive symptoms were assessed through the Subjective Memory Complaints Questionnaire (SMCQ), and caregiverreported cognitive decline was evaluated using the Seoul Informant Report Questionnaire for Dementia (SIRQD) . Psychological and somatic symptom assessments included the Hospital Anxiety and Depression Scale (HADS) to evaluate anxiety and depressive symptoms; the Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index (PSQI) global score, which is the sum of component scores, to assess overall sleep quality; and the Patient Health Questionnaire-15 (PHQ-15) to gauge the burden of somatic symptoms . Preoperative pain intensity was assessed using the Numeric Rating Scale (NRS). The primary /uniFB01 ndings of this prospective cohort study are that lower preoperative MMSE scores and higher PHQ-15 scores signi /uniFB01 cantly predicted POD in patients undergoing TKA. The reported incidence of POD following TKA varies considerably, with rates ranging from 0% to 0.7% in fasttrack arthroplasty registry data to 3.1% to 6.5% in single-center cohorts and up to 1.5% to 7.1% in studies involving total joint arthroplasty populations that include both TKA and total hip arthroplasty (THA) . POD manifests as acute confusion, inattention, and /uniFB02 uctuating mental status, resulting in increased hospital stay length, morbidity, and health-care expenses . Considering its impact on postoperative recovery and outcomes, the identi /uniFB01 cation of modi /uniFB01 able risk factors for POD is necessary.

A prospective cohort study design was implemented to recruit patients undergoing primary TKA at major tertiary care centers from May 2021 to December 2024. These facilities adhered to comparable hospitalization standards and operational techniques for patients who underwent TKA, enhancing consistency in perioperative management.

The hospitals ' institutional review board approved the study (no. 2305-138-1434).

The study enrolled patients who were ‡ 60 years of age and were scheduled for primary TKA due to degenerative osteoarthritis, con /uniFB01 rmed by a Kellgren-Lawrence grade of ‡ 3

on radiographic evaluation. Patients were excluded if they had a clinical diagnosis of dementia, were taking dementiarelated medication, or were considered unsuitable for participation by the principal investigator.

Demographic and clinical data included age, body mass index (BMI), sex, history of delirium, comorbidities (e.g., hypertension, diabetes mellitus, chronic kidney disease, cerebrovascular disease, and solid tumor), and the Charlson Comorbidity Index (CCI). The use of glasses or hearing aids was documented. Socioeconomic factors, including education level, employment status, medical coverage type, marital and parental status, history of alcohol use, and history of smoking, were documented.

Laboratory evaluations included hemoglobin, blood urea nitrogen (BUN), creatinine, estimated glomerular /uniFB01 ltration rate (eGFR), albumin, sodium, potassium, erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR), and C-reactive protein (CRP) .

The use of preoperative medications, including opioids, sedatives, antidepressants, antipsychotics, antiepileptics, cholinergic agents, and anticholinergic agents, was also documented .

Regarding environmental conditions, noise levels were measured before and after the preoperative interview, and the mean of these levels was used for analysis. A sound level meter placed m from the patient ' s bed recorded the noise in decibels (dB). Illuminance (lux) levels in the patient ' s hospital room and the bed ' s position relative to the window were recorded.

Differences in continuous variables were assessed using the independent t test, and categorical variables were analyzed with the chi-square test. Variables demonstrating signi /uniFB01 cant differences between the groups in univariate analyses were checked for multicollinearity, de /uniFB01 ned as a tolerance of <0.2 or variance in /uniFB02 ation factor (VIF) of >5, and were excluded from the logistic regression analysis if multicollinearity was present . Multivariable logistic regression analyses were conducted to identify signi /uniFB01 cant risk factors for POD. Additionally, odds ratios (ORs), along with 95% con /uniFB01 dence intervals (CIs), were calculated. Based on clinical relevance and consideration of multicollinearity, potential confounders (e.g., age, BMI, CCI, noise level, and pain NRS) were adjusted for in the logistic regression models . Receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve analyses were performed to determine the optimal cutoff values for MMSE, PSQI, and PHQ-15 scores in predicting POD. The Youden index was used to identify the point maximizing sensitivity and speci /uniFB01 city, and the area under the curve (AUC) and corresponding p values were calculated. A 2-tailed p value of <0.05 was considered signi /uniFB01 cant for all analyses. Statistical analyses were conducted using

## Incidence of POD

P OD occurred in (4.2%) of patients, as detailed in the patient /uniFB02 owchart (Fig. 1). Among these patients, 17 experienced delirium on the day of surgery and developed it on postoperative day 1, with onset at a mean of 0.29 ± 0.46 days.

Regarding the psychological factors, the POD group exhibited higher PSQI scores (11.05 ± 4.17 compared with 8.40 ± 3.93; p = 0.014) and PHQ-15 scores (5.92 ± 3.21 compared with 4.28 ± 2.57; p = 0.014).

Postoperative evaluations were conducted daily from postoperative days to by trained research evaluators. All patients were screened using standardized tools: the A ' s Test (4AT: Arousal, Attention, Abbreviated Mental Test-4, Acute change) and the Confusion Assessment Method (CAM) . POD was de /uniFB01 ned as a CAM-positive result (see Appendix Supplementary Table 1). The Delirium Rating Scalerevised-98 was administered to patients who scored positive on the 4AT but did not meet CAM criteria, in order to identify subsyndromal delirium . Surgical data included American Society of Anesthesiologists (ASA) classi /uniFB01 cation, anesthesia type (general or spinal), and intraoperative transfusion history. General anesthesia was administered only when spinal anesthesia was contraindicated, such as in patients taking antiplatelet medications that could not be discontinued, after consultation with the anesthesiology team. Intraoperative analgesia was provided by periarticular injection administered before implantation . Postoperative pain management followed a standardized multimodal analgesic protocol, consisting of scheduled non-opioid analgesics and a continuous adductor canal block using an indwelling catheter maintained until postoperative day 3, with opioids provided only as rescue medication when necessary. This study had several limitations. First, although the study was executed at major tertiary care hospitals with similar hospitalization protocols and surgical procedures for patients who underwent TKA, these /uniFB01 ndings may have limited generalizability to institutions with different perioperative management strategies. In particular, because all patients were admitted the day prior to surgery, variations in admission practices and duration across institutions may further restrict the applicability of our results to other clinical settings. Second, the relatively small sample size of the group with POD may have reduced statistical power, potentially limiting the ability to detect other contributing factors. Although a post hoc power analysis indicated suf /uniFB01 cient power to detect correlations with an OR of 3.0, the ability to identify smaller effects may have been limited. Third, psychological assessments, including the PSQI and PHQ-15, relied on selfreported measures, which could be susceptible to response bias. More objective measures such as actigraphy for sleep monitoring or physiological stress markers may provide a more comprehensive understanding of their role in POD risk. Lastly, environmental factors, including noise and illuminance levels, were assessed on a single preoperative day and may not have fully captured the dynamic nature of hospital environments during the perioperative period. In conclusion, this prospective study comprehensively evaluated preoperative cognitive function and psychological symptoms in patients undergoing TKA. This study aimed to evaluate the correlation of preoperative cognitive and psychological factors with POD after TKA. Methods: This prospective cohort study included patients who were ‡ 60 years of age and underwent primary TKA at of major tertiary care hospitals. Psychological assessments were conducted with the Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index (PSQI), the Patient Health Questionnaire-15 (PHQ-15), and the Hospital Anxiety and Depression Scale (HADS). POD was evaluated daily from postoperative days to using the A ' s Test (4AT) and the Confusion Assessment Method (CAM). In the receiver operating characteristic curve analysis, the optimal cutoff value for predicting POD was an MMSE score of £ 25, with a sensitivity of 74.5% and a speci /uniFB01 city of 78.3% (area under the curve, 0.834; p = 0.001). Although cognitive impairment is a well-established risk factor for POD, most studies have relied on brief assessments such as the Mini-Mental State Examination (MMSE), which fail to capture the full spectrum of cognitive functions . Additionally, preoperative psychological symptoms such as sleep disturbances, anxiety, and depression have been linked to an increased risk of POD . Given the high prevalence of these conditions among elderly patients undergoing TKA , a comprehensive assessment of cognitive and psychological functions is crucial for identifying modi /uniFB01 able preoperative risk factors and developing targeted interventions to prevent POD . Recent systematic reviews have further underscored this need, emphasizing the multifactorial nature of POD and noting that most available evidence derives from heterogeneous surgical cohorts rather than TKA populations speci /uniFB01 cally . Consequently, in this study we hypothesized that speci /uniFB01 c aspects of cognitive and psychological functions may increase the risk of POD in patients undergoing TKA. Additionally, it evaluated preoperative cognitive and psychological functions and their correlation with POD, while integrating a comprehensive spectrum of potential risk factors, such as comorbidities, laboratory /uniFB01 ndings, baseline medication usage, and environmental factors. Materials and Methods The attending physicians reviewed each patient ' s medical history, explained the study to them, and obtained their informed consent day prior to surgery. On the same day, research evaluators who had undergone standardized training from the principal investigator conducted cognitive and psychological assessments. These evaluators also collected demographic and clinical information, data on socioeconomic factors, laboratory results, and environmental conditions before surgery. Cognitive function was evaluated using the Korean version of the Consortium to Establish a Registry for Alzheimer ' s Disease (CERAD) neuropsychological battery, which comprises tests: J1 (Verbal Fluency), J2 (Boston Naming Test), J3 (MMSE), J4 (Wordlist Learning), J5 (Constructional Praxis), J6 (Wordlist Recall), J7 (Wordlist Recognition), J8 (Constructional Praxis Recall), and J9 (Trail Making Test, Parts A and B) . The CERAD total II score was calculated by summing the J1, J2, J4, J5, J6, J7, and J8 scores. Subjective cognitive symptoms were assessed through the Subjective Memory Complaints Questionnaire (SMCQ), and caregiverreported cognitive decline was evaluated using the Seoul Informant Report Questionnaire for Dementia (SIRQD) . Psychological and somatic symptom assessments included the Hospital Anxiety and Depression Scale (HADS) to evaluate anxiety and depressive symptoms; the Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index (PSQI) global score, which is the sum of component scores, to assess overall sleep quality; and the Patient Health Questionnaire-15 (PHQ-15) to gauge the burden of somatic symptoms . Preoperative pain intensity was assessed using the Numeric Rating Scale (NRS). The primary /uniFB01 ndings of this prospective cohort study are that lower preoperative MMSE scores and higher PHQ-15 scores signi /uniFB01 cantly predicted POD in patients undergoing TKA. ## Incidence of POD

P OD occurred in (4.2%) of patients, as detailed in the patient /uniFB02 owchart (Fig. 1). Among these patients, 17 experienced delirium on the day of surgery and developed it on postoperative day 1, with onset at a mean of 0.29 ± 0.46 days.

Regarding the psychological factors, the POD group exhibited higher PSQI scores (11.05 ± 4.17 compared with 8.40 ± 3.93; p = 0.014) and PHQ-15 scores (5.92 ± 3.21 compared with 4.28 ± 2.57; p = 0.014).

Postoperative evaluations were conducted daily from postoperative days to by trained research evaluators. All patients were screened using standardized tools: the A ' s Test (4AT: Arousal, Attention, Abbreviated Mental Test-4, Acute change) and the Confusion Assessment Method (CAM) . POD was de /uniFB01 ned as a CAM-positive result (see Appendix Supplementary Table 1). General anesthesia was administered only when spinal anesthesia was contraindicated, such as in patients taking antiplatelet medications that could not be discontinued, after consultation with the anesthesiology team. Intraoperative analgesia was provided by periarticular injection administered before implantation . Postoperative pain management followed a standardized multimodal analgesic protocol, consisting of scheduled non-opioid analgesics and a continuous adductor canal block using an indwelling catheter maintained until postoperative day 3, with opioids provided only as rescue medication when necessary. The group with POD, compared with the group without POD, had a higher CCI (3.39 ± 2.21 compared with 1.96 ± 1.77; p = 0.010) and more frequent use of sedatives (16.7% compared with 6.5%; p = 0.044) and antidepressants (12.5% compared with 3.8%; p = 0.027). The mean noise level was lower in the group with POD (50.5 ± 7.4 compared with 56.4 ± 15.2 dB; p = 0.002). The results of the CERAD subtests and psychological assessments are presented in Appendix Supplementary Table 3. High background noise has been recognized as a potential contributor to delirium, particularly in intensive care unit settings, which can disrupt normal sleep-wake cycles . However, our study revealed that the group with POD experienced lower preoperative noise levels compared with the group without POD. The World Health Organizationrecommended maximum of dB for patient rooms was exceeded in both groups, indicating exposure to relatively high noise levels . After adjustment for covariates, noise level was not independently correlated with POD. Given that measurements were taken in the general ward on the day before surgery, the observed difference might re /uniFB02 ect transient variations in environmental conditions rather than a protective or harmful effect of noise itself. By employing the complete CERAD neuropsychological battery, this study facilitated a more thorough assessment of cognitive function across multiple domains. The CERAD battery assesses multiple cognitive domains, such as verbal memory, executive function, visuospatial skills, and recognition memory, and is widely recognized for its ef /uniFB01 cacy in detecting cognitive impairments and Alzheimer disease . Nonetheless, due to the high intercorrelation among CERAD subtests, it was not possible to include all variables in the /uniFB01 nal logistic regression model, to avoid multicollinearity. Previous studies have shown that the CERAD total score offers superior diagnostic accuracy over the MMSE in differentiating among normal aging, mild cognitive impairment, and Alzheimer disease . However, in our study, the difference in the CERAD total II score between the group with POD and the group without POD did not reach signi /uniFB01 cance in univariate analysis (p = 0.072). The SMCQ, which assesses subjective cognitive function from the patient perspective, and SIRQD, which assesses subjective cognitive function from the caregiver perspective, did not correlate with POD risk in our cohort. This indicates that objective cognitive assessments may offer stronger predictive value compared with subjective evaluations in the TKA population. hc_limitations:
This study had several limitations. First, although the study was executed at major tertiary care hospitals with similar hospitalization protocols and surgical procedures for patients who underwent TKA, these /uniFB01 ndings may have limited generalizability to institutions with different perioperative management strategies. In particular, because all patients were admitted the day prior to surgery, variations in admission practices and duration across institutions may further restrict the applicability of our results to other clinical settings. Second, the relatively small sample size of the group with POD may have reduced statistical power, potentially limiting the ability to detect other contributing factors. Although a post hoc power analysis indicated suf /uniFB01 cient power to detect correlations with an OR of 3.0, the ability to identify smaller effects may have been limited. Third, psychological assessments, including the PSQI and PHQ-15, relied on selfreported measures, which could be susceptible to response bias. More objective measures such as actigraphy for sleep monitoring or physiological stress markers may provide a more comprehensive understanding of their role in POD risk. Lastly, environmental factors, including noise and illuminance levels, were assessed on a single preoperative day and may not have fully captured the dynamic nature of hospital environments during the perioperative period. In conclusion, this prospective study comprehensively evaluated preoperative cognitive function and psychological symptoms in patients undergoing TKA. ## Clinical Outcomes After and 2-Level Lumbar Total Disc Arthroplasty

1,187 Patients with to 21-Year Follow-up

Thierry P. Marnay, MD, Guillaume Y. Geneste, MD, Gregory W. Edgard-Rosa, MD, Martin M. Grau-Ortiz, MD, Caroline C. Hirsch, MD, and Georges G. Negre, MD

Investigation performed at Montpellier Spine Institute (CCV) Clinique du Parc, Castelnau-le-Lez, France

Background: In this study, we expand the supportive evidence for total disc arthroplasty (TDA) with results up to years in a large patient cohort who received a semiconstrained ball-and-socket lumbar prosthesis. The objectives of the study were to compare the results for versus 2-level surgeries and to evaluate whether prior surgery at the index level(s) impacts clinical outcomes.

Methods: From 1999 to 2013, 1,187 patients with chronic lumbar degenerative disc disease (DDD) underwent lumbar TDA, of whom underwent a 1-level procedure and underwent a 2-level procedure. A total of (31.4%) of the patients had prior index-level surgery. Patients were evaluated preoperatively; at 3, 6, 12, 18, and months postoperatively; and yearly thereafter. The follow-up duration ranged from to years (mean, 11 years and months). Collected data included radiographic, neurological, and physical assessments, as well as self-evaluations using the Oswestry Disability Index (ODI) and visual analog scale (VAS) for back and leg pain. Perioperative data points, complication rates, and reoperation or revision rates were also assessed. Patients were divided into groups: 1-level TDA with no prior surgery at the index level, 1-level TDA with prior surgery, 2-level TDA with no prior surgery, and 2-level TDA with prior surgery.

Results: All groups showed dramatic reduction in the ODI at months postoperatively and maintained these scores over time. Although VAS pain did not diminish to its /uniFB01 nal level as rapidly for patients with prior surgery, there was no signi /uniFB01 cant difference betweenthegroupsintermsofpain reduction at months postoperatively. Of patients, 49 (4.13%) required either a new surgery at another level or revision or reoperation at the index level. Rates were too low in all groups to compare them statistically. Total TDA revision and adjacent-level surgery rates over to years were very low (0.67% and 1.85%, respectively).

Conclusions: This study demonstrates the robust long-term clinical success of and 2-level lumbar TDA as assessed at to years postoperatively in one of the largest evaluated cohorts of patients with TDA. Patients had dramatic and maintained reductions in disability and pain scores over time and low rates of index-level revision or reoperation and adjacent-level surgery relative to published long-term fusion data. Additionally, patients who underwent 1-level lumbar TDA and those who underwent 2level TDA demonstrated equivalent improvement, as did patients with prior surgery at the index level and those with no prior surgery.

Level of Evidence: Therapeutic Level III. See Instructions for Authors for a complete description of levels of evidence.

Improvements in surgical techniques and implant design fueled the rapid expansion of fusion procedures for the treatment of DDD, including in patients with recurrent disc herniation, post-discectomy syndrome, and/or multilevel pathology.

However, less-than-perfect lumbar spinal fusion rates have been shown to contribute to poorer outcomes and relatively high rates of complications, including pseudarthrosis , device failure , and post-fusion comorbidities . Research has shown that fusion also reduces spinal mobility and affects the natural instantaneous adaptation of the spine to position changes, including spinal balance . Multiple studies have also clearly shown that fusion is associated with accelerated degeneration and symptomatic disease at adjacent levels, which ultimately leads to high reoperation rates . These and other similar reports, however, did not slow the exponential growth of spinal fusion. Instead, what should have been a last-choice surgical treatment became a ' gold standard ' procedure.

Nevertheless, motion-preserving devices showed early success during this period , with the promise of mitigating the aforementioned key issues associated with fusion while enabling the restoration of lumbar mobility in /uniFB02 exion-extension, lateral bending, and axial rotation. In 2005, Tropiano et al. reported the to 11-year outcomes of patients who underwent /uniFB01 rstgeneration lumbar disc replacement with the prodisc I (J.B.S., Troyes, France) between 1990 and 1993 13,14 . The authors demonstrated signi /uniFB01 cant early and long-lasting reduction in disability and in back and leg pain and reported good or excellent results (using the modi /uniFB01 ed Stauffer-Coventry score 15 ) in 78% of patients, with no evidence of loosening, migration, or implant failure. In the same cohort, Huang et al. demonstrated the quality of long-term /uniFB02 exion-extension mobility at the operative levels and a clear relationship between motion restoration and preservation of the adjacent levels over an 8-year period . The device was improved in 1999, although the mechanism of action -a semiconstrained ball-and-socket joint with a /uniFB01 xed polyethylene core and center of rotation -remained the same. The second-generation implant was released to expanded clinical usage, which allowed a new study by the Montpellier Spine Institute (Centre de Chirurgie Vert´ ebrale de Montpellier) . In 2001, the device was entered into U.S. Food and Drug Administration Investigational Device Exemption (IDE) studies comparing and 2-level arthroplasty to 360 /C176 fusion.

The U.S. IDE studies showed excellent patient-reported outcomes and a lower reoperation rate at both the index and adjacent levels. Zigler et al. reported that the rate of adjacent segment degeneration at years after TDA was dramatically lower than that after fusion . Delamarter et al. 22 and Hannibal et al. 23 reported similar results for 2-level DDD and showed no signi /uniFB01 cant difference between and 2-level surgeries. Bertagnoli et al. 24 and Trincat et al. 25 con /uniFB01 rmed the clinical success of and 2-level TDA over to years of followup. Somewhat unexpectedly, many of these studies also showed

The breadth of publications and the quality of the results provide strong evidence that lumbar TDA is superior to fusion for the treatment of lumbar degenerative disease , that it is as effective in treating 2-level disease as it is for 1-level disease, and that it is effective for patients with failed or repeated prior discectomy. However, long-term published data are limited, which has affected the wider acceptance of lumbar TDA. The present study was designed to present the clinical outcomes of patients with or without a prior discectomy at the index level(s) who underwent or 2-level TDA for DDD and had long-term follow-up between and years. The objectives of this study were to determine if there were differences in outcomes between patients who underwent versus 2-level TDA as well as between patients with no prior surgery versus those with a prior discectomy. This study of the data of patients covered all eligible and 2-level TDAs performed at a single institution.

The percentage of improvement between the preoperative time point and the 24-month follow-up remained superior, in the range of 50% to 60%, in all groups for all measures until the last follow-up (Fig. 9).

The rates of revision or reoperation and new surgery were low (and too low for statistical comparisons) and involved only (4.13%) of the patients (Table VI). Ten patients required posterior decompression. Nine patients underwent reoperation for hematoma or surgical wound complication. Eight patients (0.67%) required revision of the implant at the index level: 1 underwent posterior fusion, 4 underwent a new disc implantation, and underwent anterior lumbar interbody fusion. Most of the revisions at the index level were in Group and occurred during the earliest part of the clinical series due to mis-centering, vertebral body fracture, or an unlocked polyethylene core. Twenty-two (1.85%) of the patients had undergone a new surgery at the adjacent level by the time of the last follow-up.

## Discussion

T he surgical treatment of intractable back pain associated with lumbar DDD took a revolutionary turn in 1990 with the introduction of TDA. At that time, there were several unanswered questions regarding TDA, speci /uniFB01 cally in terms of device and surgical safety, the ef /uniFB01 cacy of TDA in treating low back pain, the capacity of TDA to treat associated leg pain, the value of the procedure for not only level but also multiple levels, and the effectiveness of TDA after an unsuccessful discectomy. As a total joint replacement procedure, the longevity of both the device and the clinical results was also an essential question. Preservation of the adjacent levels after TDA also had yet to be proven through a long-term follow-up study.

The /uniFB01 rst medium-term follow-up analysis by Tropiano et al. 13 and the radiographic results reported by Huang et al. 16 answered the /uniFB01 rst question, demonstrating that the device and the procedure are safe and effective. Multiple studies have con /uniFB01 rmed these /uniFB01 ndings . For the remaining questions, Huang et al. demonstrated that restoring mobility has a direct correlation with the quality of the clinical outcomes and protection of the adjacent levels . Zigler et al. con /uniFB01 rmed that the adjacent levels were protected after TDA at years of follow-up . During the last years, Delamarter et al. 22 and Trincat et al. 25 demonstrated that the results of 2-level TDA were superior to those of 2-level fusion. These studies also demonstrated equivalent results between and 2-level TDA.

We de /uniFB01 ned fundamental technical rules that align with the conclusions of Park et al. 31 , who experienced a challenging learning curve (an implant-related complication rate of 9.3%): (1) adequate bone quality (DXA T-score ‡ 2 1.0) is important, (2) the implant must be carefully centered, (3) the anterior release must be meticulously performed, (4) keel-cut chiseling should be monitored under lateral /uniFB02 uoroscopy to ensure that the superior vertebral body cut is as deep as the inferior cut, and (5) polyethylene inlay locking should be con /uniFB01 rmed both tactilely and visually. In our study, following these rules, revisions occurred in only 0.49% of implants (Table VI).

As noted previously, adjacent-level degeneration is one of the critical points to study for any lumbar surgery, as it determines the long-term ef /uniFB01 cacy of the surgery. The adjacent-level degeneration rate in the present study was higher in the groups with prior surgery (Groups and 4) than in the groups without. This difference can be explained by the long delay (the time from the initial signs to the /uniFB01 rst discectomy to the TDA) before the restoration of mobility at the index level in Groups and 4. When following these recommendations regarding the type of access, careful selection of patients, and the technical rules for implantation, it is obvious that, as in all surgery, training and experienced mentors are key to a low complication rate.

## Limitations

This was a retrospective study. Patients were selected for TDA by experienced anterior lumbar spine surgeons according to the indications and contraindications mentioned above. We analyzed a large cohort of patients at up to 21-year follow-up. Our follow-up rate at months (83.6% [992 of patients]) is higher than that in prior long-term studies. However, later follow-up rates declined for the usual or natural

reasons (e.g., no response, moved without providing the new address, deceased, not interested in being contacted). Theoretically, those patients who were lost to longer-term follow-up might have had poorer results than the rest of the group; however, it is just as likely that they did not return because they were experiencing satisfactory results.

The natural history (aging process) of the joints, especially in the spine, should also be taken into consideration in the analysis of the patient-reported outcomes. Despite these limitations, the present study is the /uniFB01 rst of its kind in the literature to evaluate such a large cohort of patients who underwent lumbar TDA with such a long duration of followup.

## Conclusions

In a study of one of the largest TDA cohorts to date, we found equivalent improvement between patients who underwent 1level lumbar TDA and those who underwent 2-level TDA, as well as between patients with prior surgery at the index level and patients with no prior surgery. This study also demonstrated the robust long-term clinical success and durability of and 2-level lumbar TDA, as assessed at to years postoperatively. Patients had dramatic and maintained reductions in disability and pain scores over time and low rates of indexlevel revision or reoperation and adjacent-level surgery. n

Background: In this study, we expand the supportive evidence for total disc arthroplasty (TDA) with results up to years in a large patient cohort who received a semiconstrained ball-and-socket lumbar prosthesis. The objectives of the study were to compare the results for versus 2-level surgeries and to evaluate whether prior surgery at the index level(s) impacts clinical outcomes.

Methods: From 1999 to 2013, 1,187 patients with chronic lumbar degenerative disc disease (DDD) underwent lumbar TDA, of whom underwent a 1-level procedure and underwent a 2-level procedure. A total of (31.4%) of the patients had prior index-level surgery. Patients were evaluated preoperatively; at 3, 6, 12, 18, and months postoperatively; and yearly thereafter. The follow-up duration ranged from to years (mean, 11 years and months). Collected data included radiographic, neurological, and physical assessments, as well as self-evaluations using the Oswestry Disability Index (ODI) and visual analog scale (VAS) for back and leg pain. Perioperative data points, complication rates, and reoperation or revision rates were also assessed. Patients were divided into groups: 1-level TDA with no prior surgery at the index level, 1-level TDA with prior surgery, 2-level TDA with no prior surgery, and 2-level TDA with prior surgery.

Results: All groups showed dramatic reduction in the ODI at months postoperatively and maintained these scores over time. Although VAS pain did not diminish to its /uniFB01 nal level as rapidly for patients with prior surgery, there was no signi /uniFB01 cant difference betweenthegroupsintermsofpain reduction at months postoperatively. Of patients, 49 (4.13%) required either a new surgery at another level or revision or reoperation at the index level. Rates were too low in all groups to compare them statistically. Total TDA revision and adjacent-level surgery rates over to years were very low (0.67% and 1.85%, respectively).

Conclusions: This study demonstrates the robust long-term clinical success of and 2-level lumbar TDA as assessed at to years postoperatively in one of the largest evaluated cohorts of patients with TDA. Patients had dramatic and maintained reductions in disability and pain scores over time and low rates of index-level revision or reoperation and adjacent-level surgery relative to published long-term fusion data. Additionally, patients who underwent 1-level lumbar TDA and those who underwent 2level TDA demonstrated equivalent improvement, as did patients with prior surgery at the index level and those with no prior surgery.

Improvements in surgical techniques and implant design fueled the rapid expansion of fusion procedures for the treatment of DDD, including in patients with recurrent disc herniation, post-discectomy syndrome, and/or multilevel pathology.

However, less-than-perfect lumbar spinal fusion rates have been shown to contribute to poorer outcomes and relatively high rates of complications, including pseudarthrosis , device failure , and post-fusion comorbidities . Research has shown that fusion also reduces spinal mobility and affects the natural instantaneous adaptation of the spine to position changes, including spinal balance . Multiple studies have also clearly shown that fusion is associated with accelerated degeneration and symptomatic disease at adjacent levels, which ultimately leads to high reoperation rates . These and other similar reports, however, did not slow the exponential growth of spinal fusion. Instead, what should have been a last-choice surgical treatment became a ' gold standard ' procedure.

Nevertheless, motion-preserving devices showed early success during this period , with the promise of mitigating the aforementioned key issues associated with fusion while enabling the restoration of lumbar mobility in /uniFB02 exion-extension, lateral bending, and axial rotation. In 2005, Tropiano et al. reported the to 11-year outcomes of patients who underwent /uniFB01 rstgeneration lumbar disc replacement with the prodisc I (J.B.S., Troyes, France) between 1990 and 1993 13,14 . The authors demonstrated signi /uniFB01 cant early and long-lasting reduction in disability and in back and leg pain and reported good or excellent results (using the modi /uniFB01 ed Stauffer-Coventry score 15 ) in 78% of patients, with no evidence of loosening, migration, or implant failure. In the same cohort, Huang et al. demonstrated the quality of long-term /uniFB02 exion-extension mobility at the operative levels and a clear relationship between motion restoration and preservation of the adjacent levels over an 8-year period . The device was improved in 1999, although the mechanism of action -a semiconstrained ball-and-socket joint with a /uniFB01 xed polyethylene core and center of rotation -remained the same. The second-generation implant was released to expanded clinical usage, which allowed a new study by the Montpellier Spine Institute (Centre de Chirurgie Vert´ ebrale de Montpellier) . In 2001, the device was entered into U.S. Food and Drug Administration Investigational Device Exemption (IDE) studies comparing and 2-level arthroplasty to 360 /C176 fusion.

The U.S. IDE studies showed excellent patient-reported outcomes and a lower reoperation rate at both the index and adjacent levels. Zigler et al. reported that the rate of adjacent segment degeneration at years after TDA was dramatically lower than that after fusion . Delamarter et al. 22 and Hannibal et al. 23 reported similar results for 2-level DDD and showed no signi /uniFB01 cant difference between and 2-level surgeries. Bertagnoli et al. 24 and Trincat et al. 25 con /uniFB01 rmed the clinical success of and 2-level TDA over to years of followup. Somewhat unexpectedly, many of these studies also showed

The breadth of publications and the quality of the results provide strong evidence that lumbar TDA is superior to fusion for the treatment of lumbar degenerative disease , that it is as effective in treating 2-level disease as it is for 1-level disease, and that it is effective for patients with failed or repeated prior discectomy. However, long-term published data are limited, which has affected the wider acceptance of lumbar TDA. The present study was designed to present the clinical outcomes of patients with or without a prior discectomy at the index level(s) who underwent or 2-level TDA for DDD and had long-term follow-up between and years. The objectives of this study were to determine if there were differences in outcomes between patients who underwent versus 2-level TDA as well as between patients with no prior surgery versus those with a prior discectomy. This study of the data of patients covered all eligible and 2-level TDAs performed at a single institution.

## Discussion

T he surgical treatment of intractable back pain associated with lumbar DDD took a revolutionary turn in 1990 with the introduction of TDA. At that time, there were several unanswered questions regarding TDA, speci /uniFB01 cally in terms of device and surgical safety, the ef /uniFB01 cacy of TDA in treating low back pain, the capacity of TDA to treat associated leg pain, the value of the procedure for not only level but also multiple levels, and the effectiveness of TDA after an unsuccessful discectomy. As a total joint replacement procedure, the longevity of both the device and the clinical results was also an essential question. Preservation of the adjacent levels after TDA also had yet to be proven through a long-term follow-up study.

The /uniFB01 rst medium-term follow-up analysis by Tropiano et al. 13 and the radiographic results reported by Huang et al. 16 answered the /uniFB01 rst question, demonstrating that the device and the procedure are safe and effective. Multiple studies have con /uniFB01 rmed these /uniFB01 ndings . For the remaining questions, Huang et al. demonstrated that restoring mobility has a direct correlation with the quality of the clinical outcomes and protection of the adjacent levels . Zigler et al. con /uniFB01 rmed that the adjacent levels were protected after TDA at years of follow-up . During the last years, Delamarter et al. 22 and Trincat et al. 25 demonstrated that the results of 2-level TDA were superior to those of 2-level fusion. These studies also demonstrated equivalent results between and 2-level TDA.

In cases of recurrent disc herniation, anterior transdiscal decompression is a true salvage procedure; unlike posterior decompression, the anterior approach enables decompression of the nerve without traction and thus avoids causing additional surgical injury. Further, removing all of the degenerated disc material avoids chemical toxicity in the roots from acidic disc degeneration, cytokines, and prostaglandin-B toxicity. These advantages point to the ef /uniFB01 cacy of the transdiscal approach for recurrent decompression.

In the present study, the mean percentage of improvement was between 50% and 60% in all groups for each of the criteria (ODI, VAS back pain, and VAS leg pain), which is comparable with the IDE study.

There were preconceived ideas regarding TDA and speci /uniFB01 cally the prodisc L implant that were debunked in the present study. First, we found that the /uniFB01 xed-core design of the disc provided long-term implant survivorship, as was also noted by Park et al. 31 , who reported no device failure over a 10-year period. Second, this design and the mobility that it provided protected the adjacent levels in the long term, which contrasts with the /uniFB01 ndings reported for fusion in the literature as was described by Zigler et al. in their 5-year follow-up study . TDA at levels had equivalent results to TDA at level over the long term, con /uniFB01 rming the results of the and 2-level IDE studies already published . TDA may be safely and effectively utilized in patients with recurrent disc herniation or post-discectomy syndrome: the long-term results for both and 2-level procedures in these patients were equivalent to those in patients who did not have a prior surgery. We de /uniFB01 ned fundamental technical rules that align with the conclusions of Park et al. 31 , who experienced a challenging learning curve (an implant-related complication rate of 9.3%): (1) adequate bone quality (DXA T-score ‡ 2 1.0) is important, (2) the implant must be carefully centered, (3) the anterior release must be meticulously performed, (4) keel-cut chiseling should be monitored under lateral /uniFB02 uoroscopy to ensure that the superior vertebral body cut is as deep as the inferior cut, and (5) polyethylene inlay locking should be con /uniFB01 rmed both tactilely and visually. In our study, following these rules, revisions occurred in only 0.49% of implants (Table VI).

As noted previously, adjacent-level degeneration is one of the critical points to study for any lumbar surgery, as it determines the long-term ef /uniFB01 cacy of the surgery. The adjacent-level degeneration rate in the present study was higher in the groups with prior surgery (Groups and 4) than in the groups without. This difference can be explained by the long delay (the time from the initial signs to the /uniFB01 rst discectomy to the TDA) before the restoration of mobility at the index level in Groups and 4. When following these recommendations regarding the type of access, careful selection of patients, and the technical rules for implantation, it is obvious that, as in all surgery, training and experienced mentors are key to a low complication rate.

## Limitations

This was a retrospective study. Patients were selected for TDA by experienced anterior lumbar spine surgeons according to the indications and contraindications mentioned above. We analyzed a large cohort of patients at up to 21-year follow-up. Our follow-up rate at months (83.6% [992 of patients]) is higher than that in prior long-term studies. However, later follow-up rates declined for the usual or natural

reasons (e.g., no response, moved without providing the new address, deceased, not interested in being contacted). Theoretically, those patients who were lost to longer-term follow-up might have had poorer results than the rest of the group; however, it is just as likely that they did not return because they were experiencing satisfactory results.

The natural history (aging process) of the joints, especially in the spine, should also be taken into consideration in the analysis of the patient-reported outcomes. Despite these limitations, the present study is the /uniFB01 rst of its kind in the literature to evaluate such a large cohort of patients who underwent lumbar TDA with such a long duration of followup.

## Conclusions

In a study of one of the largest TDA cohorts to date, we found equivalent improvement between patients who underwent 1level lumbar TDA and those who underwent 2-level TDA, as well as between patients with prior surgery at the index level and patients with no prior surgery. This study also demonstrated the robust long-term clinical success and durability of and 2-level lumbar TDA, as assessed at to years postoperatively. Patients had dramatic and maintained reductions in disability and pain scores over time and low rates of indexlevel revision or reoperation and adjacent-level surgery. n

## Patients

Between August 2016 and August 2021, a total of patients underwent hemipelvectomy with prosthetic reconstruction for oncological indications in our musculoskeletal tumor center. Thus, 25 of the patients were included in the assessment of the accuracy of implant installation (Table II).

## Prosthesis Design and Manufacture

The 3D-printed hemipelvic prosthesis was designed and manufactured in main steps, with details shown in Figure 1.

## Surgical Technique

After the tumor was routinely exposed, a distal osteotomy of the pubic and ischial rami or pubic symphysis was performed, depending on the extent of tumor invasion(Fig. 3-A and 3-B). Then, disarticulation of the sacroiliac joint was performed by gradually detaching the connected tissues using an electrotome. It should be noted that the sacroiliac joint is very wide and uneven, so it is necessary to dissect the ligamentous connection of the articular interface with an electrotome while gradually breaking it open.

The cartilage of the sacral articular interface was completely removed by curettage (Fig. 3-C). The subchondral bone was preserved to maintain the osseous strength (Fig. 3-D).

Because of the uneven surface of the sacroiliac joint, the prosthesis was seamlessly matched and installed (Fig. 3-E). The sacral tray of the prosthesis was placed to fully /uniFB01 t the ventral sacral interface to alleviate the shear force. Three to screws were inserted into the sacrum to /uniFB01 x the prosthesis as planned (Table III). For patients, ipsilateral lumbar pedicle screws were inserted at L5 for lumbosacral /uniFB01 xation to further enhance prosthetic stability (Fig. 3-E). Finally, the femoral stem prosthesis was routinely placed. The ligaments and muscles around the hip joint were reconstructed whenever possible.

## Postoperative Management

The initiation of bed-based early rehabilitation started weeks postoperatively. Full weight-bearing walking was not encouraged until months after surgery. All patients were followed for a minimum of months or until death.

The distributions of the stresses on the postoperative pelvis, prosthesis, and screws were compared in the static standing position. The overall distributions of von Mises stresses relative to implant locations, sacral screws, and lumbosacral systems among the models are shown in Figure 5.

The addition of lumbosacral /uniFB01 xation (Model versus Model 2) visibly reduced the peak stress on the sacral screws by 48.2% (from 157.1 to 81.4 MPa) (Table V). Increasing the number of sacral screws from to (Model versus Model 4) not surprisingly also alleviated the peak stress on the sacral screws by 28.4% (from 157.1 to 112.5 MPa). However, the peak stress decreased only by 11.5% (from 112.5 to 99.6 MPa) with a further increase from to screws (Model versus Model 5). Halving all screw lengths exacerbated the peak stress on the sacral screws, from 157.1 to 233.2 MPa (Model versus Model 3).

In this study, we aimed to establish a safe osteotomy margin, accurately restore the HRC, and achieve low mechanical failure via our customized prosthesis after type I II ( 1 III) internal hemipelvectomy. The use of this prosthesis has advantages. First, the 3D-printed articular interface of the prosthesis was designed to seamlessly match the irregular sacral interface. Thus, the position of the prosthesis could be uniquely determined during installation, allowing placement of the acetabular cup at the native position. The mean anteroposterior and craniocaudal displacement distances of the HRC in the present study were 5.95 and 7.29 mm, respectively, which were fully within the safe range of dislocation risk (<18 mm and <20 mm, respectively), as reported in our previous study . In addition, an acceptable dislocation rate (7.1%, 2 of 28) was identi /uniFB01 ed for the cohort, which appears to be favorable compared with the rates of most other types of reconstructions (Table VI). Second, the relatively large, seamless, and porous bone-prosthesis interface, the novel sacral tray structure, and the lumbosacral /uniFB01 xation system collectively relieved shear force and may promote osseointegration, subsequently reducing implant-related complications and leading to stable reconstruction. In this study, although the total rate of the prosthesis -related complications of aseptic loosening, prosthetic breakage, and dislocation reached 28.6% (8 of 28), this rate decreased for patients who underwent lumbosacral /uniFB01 xation (15.4%, 2 of 13) or who had or sacral screws implanted (16.7%, 3 of 18). Thus, short to medium-term mechanical complications may be able to be controlled during the process of prosthesis design and /uniFB01 xation. In addition, the rate of the prosthesis -related complication of deep infection was 7.1% (2 of 28), which is no higher than that reported for hip transposition . The rapid and relatively straightforward installation of the prosthesis could reduce the operative time and thus might reduce the infection rate. As for the porous ' boneimplant ' interface, Zhang et al. 18 reported on a series of hemipelvic reconstructions using a prosthesis with a 3D-printed porous interface and showed the occurrence of osseointegration at the bone-prosthesis interface as assessed by hard-tissue slicing and micro-CT scanning, with case requiring a second external hemipelvectomy for local recurrence. However, the evidence of osseointegration could not be captured in our cases since we have not performed a revision surgery, in which we can check the osseointegration of the bone-implant interface by pathology. Third, the number and trajectories of sacral screws were planned on an individualized basis to avoid injuring the surrounding neurovascular structures. A high degree of safety and convenience of operation were achieved during the prosthesis /uniFB01 xation process. Our newly designed prosthesis demonstrated acceptable early functional outcomes, which seemed no inferior to those reported by other studies (T able VI).

Good biomechanical properties are essential for the design of arti /uniFB01 cial implants to prevent prosthesis-related complications . In the present study, we observed that the presence of lumbosacral /uniFB01 xation or an increase in the number of sacral screws from to or decreased the risk of instrumentation failure. This result was further con /uniFB01 rmed by the /uniFB01 nite element analysis, which showed that

lumbosacral /uniFB01 xation or more sacral screws could decrease and disperse the shear force exerted on each screw. This vertical force would gradually contribute to the breakage of screws and prosthetic loosening. Similar phenomena have also been con /uniFB01 rmed by multiple studies . On the basis of these /uniFB01 ndings, we recommend the use of to sacral screws to improve the stability of prostheses in clinical practice. If there is only room to accommodate sacral screws, the use of a unilateral lumbosacral prosthesis /uniFB01 xation system is highly recommended. In addition, halving all screw lengths exacerbates the peak stress on the sacral screws. Thus, ensuring suf /uniFB01 cient sacral screw length is necessary for a stable /uniFB01 xation.

This study had a number of limitations. First, it was a retrospective study without a control group. We cannot directly compare the outcomes with available alternatives. Second, a minimum of years of follow-up is insuf /uniFB01 cient to fully assess prosthesis durability, and we will continue to follow this cohort. Third, the /uniFB01 nite element model for the biomechanical analysis was simpli /uniFB01 ed to reduce computational complexity. Only staticload analysis was incorporated into the study; gait analysis with a motion capture system should be the focus of a future study. Fourth, the follow-up duration of the lumbosacral /uniFB01 xation group was shorter than that of the group without lumbosacral /uniFB01 xation. Initially, the prosthesis was designed only for /uniFB01 xation with sacral screws. However, as relatively high aseptic loosening and prosthetic breakage rates were observed, especially when only sacral screws were used for /uniFB01 xation, the lumbosacral system was introduced and used when possible, with more stable /uniFB01 xation expected. This development of the /uniFB01 xation approach contributed to the difference in follow-up duration, which might result in bias in the mechanical failure analysis.

In summary, the use of a 3D-printed hemipelvic prosthesis could help surgeons reconstruct the HRC at the native position and lead to satisfactory functional recovery. The lumbosacral /uniFB01 xation system and more sacral screws combined with the sacral tray system worked ef /uniFB01 ciently to alleviate shear force, which may decrease the risk of prosthesis-related complications. The seamlessly matched and porous bone-prosthesis interface might achieve osseointegration and long-term stabilization.

## 3D-Printed Prosthesis with an Articular Interface for Anatomical Acetabular Reconstruction After Type I II ( 1 III) Internal Hemipelvectomy

Clinical Outcomes and Finite Element Analysis

Xin Huang, MD*, Donghua Huang, MD*, Nong Lin, MD, Xiaobo Yan, MD, Hao Qu, MD, and Zhaoming Ye, PhD

Investigation performed at the Musculoskeletal Tumor Center, Department of Orthopedics, The Second Af /uniFB01 liated Hospital of Zhejiang University School of Medicine, Hangzhou, Zhejiang, People ' s Republic of China

Background: Pelvic reconstruction after type I II (or type I II III) internal hemipelvectomy with extensive ilium removal is a great challenge. In an attempt to anatomically reconstruct the hip rotation center (HRC) and achieve a low mechanical failure rate, a custom-made, 3D-printed prosthesis with a porous articular interface was developed. The aim of this study was to investigate the clinical outcomes of patients treated with this prosthesis.

Methods: This retrospective cohort study included patients with type I II ( 1 III) internal hemipelvectomy through the articular interface of the sacroiliac joint and managed with a prosthesis at a single center between August 2016 and August 2021. Complications and oncological outcomes were analyzed. The position of the reconstructed HRC was assessed and lower-limb function was evaluated. ## Materials and Methods

## Patients

T he current study was approved by the institutional review board of our hospital (2021-0141). Between August 2016 and August 2021, a total of patients underwent hemipelvectomy with prosthetic reconstruction for oncological indications in our musculoskeletal tumor center. The general indications for this prosthesis were periacetabular tumors with extensive iliac involvement, which resulted in a lack of remaining iliac bone for conventional hemipelvic prosthesis /uniFB01 xation after tumor resection. The contraindications were (1) invasion of the sacroiliac joint by the tumor, (2) a tumor of the ilium with a huge soft-tissue mass hindering disarticulation of the sacroiliac joint, and (3) ankylosed sacroiliac joints. An extensive osteolytic lesion in the ilium near the sacroiliac joint was regarded as a relative contraindication. The process of inclusion and exclusion is shown in Figure 2. Overall, 28 patients were included in the study. The demographic and clinical characteristics are presented in Table I. Brie /uniFB02 y, there were patients with primary malignant tumors and patients with metastatic disease. According to the Enneking and Dunham classi /uniFB01 cation system , a type I II resection was carried out for patients, and a type I II III resection was performed for patients. Three patients underwent pelvic radiographic imaging only, without computed tomography (CT) scans, for various reasons. Thus, 25 of the patients were included in the assessment of the accuracy of implant installation (Table II).

## Prosthesis Design and Manufacture

The 3D-printed hemipelvic prosthesis was designed and manufactured in main steps, with details shown in Figure 1.

## Surgical Technique

After the tumor was routinely exposed, a distal osteotomy of the pubic and ischial rami or pubic symphysis was performed, depending on the extent of tumor invasion(Fig. 3-A and 3-B). Then, disarticulation of the sacroiliac joint was performed by gradually detaching the connected tissues using an electrotome. It should be noted that the sacroiliac joint is very wide and uneven, so it is necessary to dissect the ligamentous connection of the articular interface with an electrotome while gradually breaking it open.

The cartilage of the sacral articular interface was completely removed by curettage (Fig. 3-C). The subchondral bone was preserved to maintain the osseous strength (Fig. 3-D).

Because of the uneven surface of the sacroiliac joint, the prosthesis was seamlessly matched and installed (Fig. 3-E). The sacral tray of the prosthesis was placed to fully /uniFB01 t the ventral sacral interface to alleviate the shear force. Three to screws were inserted into the sacrum to /uniFB01 x the prosthesis as planned (Table III). For patients, ipsilateral lumbar pedicle screws were inserted at L5 for lumbosacral /uniFB01 xation to further enhance prosthetic stability (Fig. 3-E). Finally, the femoral stem prosthesis was routinely placed. The ligaments and muscles around the hip joint were reconstructed whenever possible.

## Postoperative Management

The initiation of bed-based early rehabilitation started weeks postoperatively. Full weight-bearing walking was not encouraged until months after surgery. All patients were followed for a minimum of months or until death.

## Accuracy of Prosthesis Placement

For of the patients analyzed, all of the sacral screws were accurately inserted into the sacral bone as assessed on CT images postoperatively. Only patient experienced a screw (at the S1 level) breaking the anterior cortical bone of the sacral canal. In this study, we aimed to establish a safe osteotomy margin, accurately restore the HRC, and achieve low mechanical failure via our customized prosthesis after type I II ( 1 III) internal hemipelvectomy. The use of this prosthesis has advantages. First, the 3D-printed articular interface of the prosthesis was designed to seamlessly match the irregular sacral interface. Thus, the position of the prosthesis could be uniquely determined during installation, allowing placement of the acetabular cup at the native position. The mean anteroposterior and craniocaudal displacement distances of the HRC in the present study were 5.95 and 7.29 mm, respectively, which were fully within the safe range of dislocation risk (<18 mm and <20 mm, respectively), as reported in our previous study . In addition, an acceptable dislocation rate (7.1%, 2 of 28) was identi /uniFB01 ed for the cohort, which appears to be favorable compared with the rates of most other types of reconstructions (Table VI). Second, the relatively large, seamless, and porous bone-prosthesis interface, the novel sacral tray structure, and the lumbosacral /uniFB01 xation system collectively relieved shear force and may promote osseointegration, subsequently reducing implant-related complications and leading to stable reconstruction. In this study, although the total rate of the prosthesis -related complications of aseptic loosening, prosthetic breakage, and dislocation reached 28.6% (8 of 28), this rate decreased for patients who underwent lumbosacral /uniFB01 xation (15.4%, 2 of 13) or who had or sacral screws implanted (16.7%, 3 of 18). Thus, short to medium-term mechanical complications may be able to be controlled during the process of prosthesis design and /uniFB01 xation. In addition, the rate of the prosthesis -related complication of deep infection was 7.1% (2 of 28), which is no higher than that reported for hip transposition . The rapid and relatively straightforward installation of the prosthesis could reduce the operative time and thus might reduce the infection rate. As for the porous ' boneimplant ' interface, Zhang et al. 18 reported on a series of hemipelvic reconstructions using a prosthesis with a 3D-printed porous interface and showed the occurrence of osseointegration at the bone-prosthesis interface as assessed by hard-tissue slicing and micro-CT scanning, with case requiring a second external hemipelvectomy for local recurrence. However, the evidence of osseointegration could not be captured in our cases since we have not performed a revision surgery, in which we can check the osseointegration of the bone-implant interface by pathology. Third, the number and trajectories of sacral screws were planned on an individualized basis to avoid injuring the surrounding neurovascular structures. A high degree of safety and convenience of operation were achieved during the prosthesis /uniFB01 xation process. Our newly designed prosthesis demonstrated acceptable early functional outcomes, which seemed no inferior to those reported by other studies (T able VI).

Good biomechanical properties are essential for the design of arti /uniFB01 cial implants to prevent prosthesis-related complications . In the present study, we observed that the presence of lumbosacral /uniFB01 xation or an increase in the number of sacral screws from to or decreased the risk of instrumentation failure. This result was further con /uniFB01 rmed by the /uniFB01 nite element analysis, which showed that

This study had a number of limitations. First, it was a retrospective study without a control group. We cannot directly compare the outcomes with available alternatives. Second, a minimum of years of follow-up is insuf /uniFB01 cient to fully assess prosthesis durability, and we will continue to follow this cohort. Third, the /uniFB01 nite element model for the biomechanical analysis was simpli /uniFB01 ed to reduce computational complexity. Only staticload analysis was incorporated into the study; gait analysis with a motion capture system should be the focus of a future study. Fourth, the follow-up duration of the lumbosacral /uniFB01 xation group was shorter than that of the group without lumbosacral /uniFB01 xation. Initially, the prosthesis was designed only for /uniFB01 xation with sacral screws. However, as relatively high aseptic loosening and prosthetic breakage rates were observed, especially when only sacral screws were used for /uniFB01 xation, the lumbosacral system was introduced and used when possible, with more stable /uniFB01 xation expected. This development of the /uniFB01 xation approach contributed to the difference in follow-up duration, which might result in bias in the mechanical failure analysis.

In summary, the use of a 3D-printed hemipelvic prosthesis could help surgeons reconstruct the HRC at the native position and lead to satisfactory functional recovery. The lumbosacral /uniFB01 xation system and more sacral screws combined with the sacral tray system worked ef /uniFB01 ciently to alleviate shear force, which may decrease the risk of prosthesis-related complications. The seamlessly matched and porous bone-prosthesis interface might achieve osseointegration and long-term stabilization.

## Outcomes Following Direct Anterior Approach Total Hip Arthroplasty

A Contemporary Multicenter Study

Jacob M. Wilson, MD, Matthew L. Hadley, MD, Dirk Larson, MS, Cameron K. Ledford, MD, Joshua S. Bingham, MD, Cody C. Wyles, MD, and Michael J. Taunton, MD

Investigation performed at the Mayo Clinic, Rochester, Minnesota

Background: The direct anterior approach (DAA) is a popular approach for primary total hip arthroplasty (THA). However, the contemporary outcomes for DAA THA need further elucidation. Therefore, we aimed to describe implant survivorship, complications, and clinical outcomes after DAA THA.

Methods: From our multi-institutional total joint registry, 3,184 patients who had undergone primary DAA THA between 2010 and 2019 were identi /uniFB01 ed. The identi /uniFB01 ed patients had a mean age of years and a mean body mass index (BMI) of kg/m , and 53% of patients were female. The indications for revision and reoperation and the incidence of complications werecollected and analyzed. Potential risk factors, including age, sex, BMI, and high-volume compared with low-volume operating surgeons, were examined. Descriptive statistics and Kaplan-Meier survivorship with Cox regression analyses were performed.

Results: At years following primary DAA THA, the cohort had 96% (95% con /uniFB01 dence interval [CI], 95% to 98%) survivorship free of any revision and 94% (95% CI, 92% to 96%) survivorship free of any reoperation. The leading indications for revision were periprosthetic joint infection (PJI) (n = 24; 5-year cumulative incidence, 0.93% [95% CI, 0.6% to 1.5%]), periprosthetic fracture (n = 20; 5-year cumulative incidence, 0.62% [95% CI, 0.4% to 1.0%]), and aseptic loosening (n = 14; 11 femoral, 3 acetabular; 5-year cumulative incidence, 0.84% [95% CI, 0.5% to 1.5%]). A BMI of ‡ 40 kg/m was found to be signi /uniFB01 cantly associated with PJI (hazard ratio [HR], 6.4; p < 0.001), reoperation (HR, 3.5; p < 0.001), and nonoperative complications (HR, 2.3; p = 0.018). Survivorship free of recurrent instability was 99.6% (95% CI, 99.4% to 99.8%) at and years, and the cumulative incidence of revision for instability was 0.14% at years.

Conclusions: In one of the largest published series to date, survivorship following DAA THA was satisfactory at early to intermediate follow-up. The leading indications for revision were PJI, periprosthetic fracture, and aseptic loosening. Instability after DAA THA was uncommon and infrequently led to revision. As a note of caution, a BMI of ‡ 40 kg/m was identi /uniFB01 ed as a risk factor for adverse outcome after DAA THA.

Level of Evidence: Therapeutic Level IV. See Instructions for Authors for a complete description of levels of evidence.

D irect anterior approach (DAA) total hip arthroplasty (THA) is now well established as a successful approach for primary THA . The utilization of this approach has increased, and a recent poll of the American Association of Hip and Knee Surgeons (AAHKS) found that nearly 50% of members are using the DAA, a sharp increase over the last decade . Although early experience with this approach was marred by high complication rates and an associated learning curve , many surgeons now have had structured training in DAA THA. Contemporary DAA THA is also facilitated by approach-speci /uniFB01 c instrumentation and implants.

Substantial effort has been employed in comparing outcomesbetween surgical approaches in primary THA . Although many approaches have been successfully utilized, there has been some indication that the reasons for failure after DAA THA may be distinct from those seen with other approaches . However,
